t.hebron al khalil old town@31.5,35.1:
Hebron, al-Khalil in Arabic, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the Middle East, set in the hills of the southern West Bank. Its heart is the old town, a warren of stone alleys, covered souqs and Mamluk-era houses, grouped around the great mosque built over the Cave of the Patriarchs, where tradition places the tombs of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives. The site is holy to Muslims, Jews and Christians, and its name in Arabic, al-Khalil, means the friend, a reference to Abraham as the friend of God.

The Old Town was inscribed by UNESCO in 2017 and immediately placed on the list of World Heritage in Danger, which says much about the situation. Hebron is a divided city, with Israeli settlements in and around the old town and a heavy military presence, and parts of the centre are closed to Palestinians, including Shuhada Street, once the main commercial street. Visiting means passing through checkpoints and encountering tension that can flare quickly. Many visitors come with a local guide or organised tour, which is wise.

The old souq is atmospheric but quieter than it once was, with many shops closed and nets strung above some alleys to catch rubbish thrown from settler buildings above. The surviving shops sell the products for which Hebron has been famous for centuries: blown glass in deep blues and greens, painted ceramics, and grapes, raisins and a thick grape syrup from the vineyards in the hills around the city.

Riding here demands serious thought. Travel advice for the West Bank changes frequently, and the situation can deteriorate quickly; check your government's guidance before going. Rental vehicles from Israel are often not insured for Palestinian areas, roads are subject to closures and checkpoints, and traffic in the city is congested and chaotic. The roads through the hills south of Bethlehem are scenic, with terraced olive groves and vineyards, but this is not a place for carefree riding.

Hebron has fuel and food. Try the local maqluba, an upside-down rice dish, or knafeh from a sweet shop.
t.sebastia@32.3,35.2:
Sebastia, Sabastiya in Arabic, is a Palestinian village on a hill north-west of Nablus, in the northern West Bank, surrounded by olive groves and terraced hillsides. It stands on the site of Samaria, the capital of the northern Kingdom of Israel in the ninth and eighth centuries BC, later rebuilt by Herod the Great, who named it Sebaste in honour of the Emperor Augustus. The ruins on the hilltop above the village span a thousand years of history.

The archaeological site includes the remains of the Israelite royal palace, a Hellenistic tower, a Roman theatre, a colonnaded street, a forum and the podium of a temple dedicated to Augustus. In the village itself stands a building that combines a Crusader cathedral with a mosque, built over a tomb associated by tradition with John the Baptist. The site is on the tentative list for UNESCO as part of the landscape of olives and vines in Palestine, and the olive groves around it are ancient.

The village depends on agriculture, especially olives, and on tourism, which has struggled because of the political situation. Access to parts of the archaeological site has been contested, and tensions between the Palestinian village and nearby Israeli settlements can flare. The situation in the northern West Bank has been especially volatile, with military operations around Nablus and Jenin.

Riding in the West Bank requires careful planning and caution. Check your government's travel advice before going, as the situation can change rapidly. Rental vehicles from Israel are often not insured for Palestinian areas, roads may be subject to checkpoints and closures, and some routes are restricted. The roads through the hills, with terraced olive groves and stone villages, are scenic, but this is not a place for a casual ride. Going with a local guide is the wisest option.

Nablus, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest major city, famous for its soap made from olive oil and for knafeh, a sweet pastry of cheese and syrup, which is said to be the best in the region. Spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers bloom, is the best time to visit.
t.necropolis of bet she arim a landmark of:
In the second century AD, after the failed revolts against Rome, the centre of Jewish life moved to Galilee, and the Sanhedrin, the supreme rabbinical council, settled for a time at Bet She'arim, on a hill at the western edge of the Jezreel valley. Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the patriarch who compiled the Mishnah, the first great codification of Jewish law, lived here, and when he was buried in the necropolis, Jews from all over the diaspora wanted to be buried near him. The result is a vast network of catacombs carved into the soft limestone, listed by UNESCO in 2015.

The catacombs are fascinating. Long corridors lead into burial halls with stone sarcophagi decorated with menorahs, lions, eagles, shells and even scenes from Greek mythology, a reminder of how deeply Jewish culture of the time was influenced by the Hellenistic world. Inscriptions in Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek and Palmyrene record the names and origins of the deceased, some from as far away as Yemen and Mesopotamia. The cave of the coffins, with more than a hundred sarcophagi, is the most impressive. The park around the catacombs is green and shady, with oak and pine trees, and it is a lovely place for a picnic.

The area around Bet She'arim is mostly suburban and agricultural, with the town of Kiryat Tivon nearby and the Jezreel valley spreading out to the east, a flat, fertile plain of fields and orchards. The roads are good but busy, and Israeli driving can be assertive. Heading north, the roads climb into the hills of Lower Galilee toward Nazareth and Tzippori, an ancient city with beautiful mosaics, and west toward Haifa and the slopes of Mount Carmel. Summers are hot and humid, winters mild with occasional rain, and spring, when the hills are green and covered in wildflowers, is the most beautiful season.

Ramat Yishay, about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Kiryat Tivon and Haifa offer more services. Before travelling, check the current security situation and travel advisories, as conditions in the region can change quickly. The site has a visitor centre and a café, and the staff can advise on the best routes through the catacombs.
t.rachid karami international fair tripoli:
In the early 1960s, the Lebanese government invited the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer to design an international fairground for Tripoli, the country's second city. He produced a vast, futuristic complex of sweeping concrete forms: a huge boomerang-shaped exhibition hall, a dome for experimental theatre, an open-air theatre, a helipad, a water tower and more, all set in a park on the edge of the city. Construction was almost finished when the civil war broke out in 1975, and the fair was never completed. Today the site stands as an extraordinary, melancholy monument to modernist ambition and lost hope, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2023, immediately placed on the list of heritage in danger.

Walking among the empty concrete structures, with weeds growing through the cracks and the sound of the city in the distance, is an unforgettable experience. The forms are elegant and daring, typical of Niemeyer's style, and they seem to float above the ground. Parts of the site have been restored, and one building has been converted into a design centre, but much remains in a state of decay.

Tripoli itself is a fascinating city, often overlooked by visitors. Its old city has one of the most important collections of Mamluk architecture in the region, with mosques, madrasas, hammams and caravanserais, and its labyrinthine souks are full of life, selling soap, gold, spices and sweets. The Citadel of Raymond de Saint-Gilles, a Crusader fortress rebuilt many times, overlooks the city. Tripoli is famous for its sweets, especially knafeh, a cheese pastry soaked in syrup, and the sweet shops are an institution.

Riding in Lebanon is chaotic, with heavy traffic, aggressive driving and few rules followed, but the rewards include stunning mountain roads, such as the climb from Tripoli to Bcharré and the Qadisha valley with its ancient cedars and rock-cut monasteries, a short ride to the southeast. Fuel and services are widely available in the city. Before travelling, check the current security situation and your government's travel advice, as conditions in Lebanon can change quickly, and some areas may be unsafe.
t.baalbek@34.0,36.2:
The stones of Baalbek are so big that for centuries people said giants or djinn must have moved them. In the trilithon, part of the foundation of the temple of Jupiter, three limestone blocks each weigh around eight hundred tonnes, and in the quarry nearby lie even larger blocks, including the Stone of the Pregnant Woman, which were cut but never moved. The Romans called the city Heliopolis, the city of the sun, and built here one of the largest temple complexes of their empire over a period of two centuries. Six columns of the temple of Jupiter still stand, about twenty metres tall, and the temple of Bacchus next to it is one of the best-preserved Roman temples anywhere, with richly carved ceilings and doorways.

Baalbek lies in the Bekaa valley, the high, fertile plain between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains, at over a thousand metres above sea level. The valley is a patchwork of fields, orchards and vineyards, and the wineries of the Bekaa, such as those around Zahle and Chtaura, produce some of the best wines in the Middle East. In summer, the Baalbek International Festival brings music and theatre to the temples, an unforgettable experience when it is held.

The road from Beirut to Baalbek crosses the Lebanon mountains over the Dahr el Baidar pass, with steep climbs, hairpins and views over the valley and the snow-capped peaks, then runs north through the Bekaa. Traffic can be heavy and chaotic, with trucks, buses and aggressive drivers, and the road surface varies. The valley is hot and dry in summer and cold in winter, with snow on the mountains.

This is also the place to be serious about safety. The Bekaa and the area around Baalbek have been affected by conflict, including air strikes in recent years, and many governments advise against travel there. Check the current situation, your government's travel advice and local conditions carefully before going. If you do go, Baalbek has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the local sfiha, small meat pies, are famous throughout Lebanon. The Hotel Palmyra, a historic hotel opposite the ruins, has hosted famous guests for over a century.
t.qalaat chama@33.1,35.2:
Before anything else: this is one of the most sensitive places on any of these routes. Qalaat Chama, or Shamaa castle, stands on a hilltop in southern Lebanon, a few kilometres north of the border with Israel and inland from Naqoura, in an area that has seen repeated conflict, including heavy fighting in recent years, and that many governments advise against visiting under any circumstances. Damage to historic sites in the area has been reported, and conditions may have changed. Do not go without checking current official travel advice, and if in doubt, do not go at all.

The castle has a long history. It dates back to the Crusader period, when the Franks built a chain of fortresses to control the coast and hinterland of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and it was later rebuilt and occupied by local rulers in the Ottoman period. Within its walls stands a shrine said to be the tomb of Shimon al-Safa, Simon Peter, the apostle, a site of pilgrimage for local people. The views from the hilltop over the hills of southern Lebanon to the Mediterranean coast are wide and beautiful.

The landscape of southern Lebanon is gentle and green, with olive groves, tobacco fields, and terraced hills dotted with villages, and in spring the hills are covered with wildflowers. The coast nearby is lined with banana plantations and beaches. Tyre, about twenty kilometres north, is one of the oldest cities in the world, with spectacular Roman ruins, including a hippodrome and a colonnaded street, listed by UNESCO, and a lively fishing harbour.

In normal times, the roads in southern Lebanon are narrow and winding, with checkpoints run by the Lebanese army and the UN peacekeeping force, UNIFIL, whose headquarters is in Naqoura. Traffic is generally light, but road conditions vary, and some areas may be closed. Fuel and services are available in Tyre and in larger villages. The food of the south is delicious: grilled fish, hummus, tabbouleh, and the sweets of Tyre. If and when peace allows, this region deserves to be visited, for its history, its landscapes and the warmth of its people.
t.baptism site bethany beyond the jordan@3:
Down here you are well below sea level, close to four hundred metres under it, and the air shows it: thick, warm and heavy, with a mineral haze rising off the Dead Sea a few kilometres to the south. The baptism site known as Bethany Beyond the Jordan, Al-Maghtas in Arabic, lies on the east bank of the river Jordan, the place many Christians identify with the baptism of Jesus by John. Across a narrow, muddy channel of water stands Qasr al-Yahud on the western side, close to Jericho, and the two banks look at each other across one of the world's most heavily watched borders.

The east bank site was listed by UNESCO in 2015. Archaeologists have uncovered Roman and Byzantine remains here: churches, baptismal pools, hermit caves and the hill associated with the prophet Elijah, who in tradition ascended to heaven from this area. Pilgrims have come since at least the Byzantine era, and you will see groups in white robes stepping into the water in many languages.

This is not a place you ride up to and park beside the river. Access is controlled, the area is a military zone, and on both sides visitors normally leave vehicles at a reception point and continue on official transport. Crossing between the two banks is only possible through the formal border crossings further north, with all the paperwork that entails. Check the current situation before you plan anything around it, because rules and openings change.

The riding around the Jordan Valley is a lesson in heat. In summer the valley floor bakes, and temperatures above forty degrees are normal, so ride early, carry far more water than you think and keep your gear vented. Winter and spring are kinder, with green patches along the river and date palms heavy with fruit. The roads are mostly straight and fast across the valley, with sharp climbs up the escarpments on either side giving views back over the river plain and the Dead Sea.

Jericho, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest real town, with fuel, food and its own long story as one of the oldest inhabited places on earth. Try the dates, drink fresh juice from a roadside stall and give yourself a quiet moment by the reeds; whatever you believe, it is a place with weight to it.
t.anjar@33.7,35.9:
In the Bekaa valley of Lebanon, close to the Syrian border, an Umayyad city lies laid out in a perfect grid, as if drawn with a ruler. Anjar was built in the early eighth century, probably under the caliph al-Walid I, as a palace town and commercial centre on the trade routes between Damascus and the coast. Its plan echoes Roman cities, with two main streets crossing at a four-sided monument, the tetrapylon, lined with the bases of hundreds of shops. Arches of the great palace, built of alternating courses of stone and brick, rise against the backdrop of the Anti-Lebanon mountains, and in the late afternoon the stone glows warm gold. The city flourished only briefly before being abandoned, which is why it is so clearly preserved. UNESCO listed it in 1984.

The modern village of Aanjar next door has a fascinating story. It was founded in 1939 by Armenian refugees from Musa Dagh, a mountain on the coast of what is now Turkey, whose people famously resisted deportation in 1915 and were rescued by French warships. Their descendants still live here, and the village has Armenian churches, schools and restaurants. Springs rise near the village, and trout restaurants beside the water are a popular weekend outing for Lebanese families.

The Bekaa is Lebanon's breadbasket, a high, fertile valley between two mountain ranges, with vineyards, orchards and fields of vegetables. It is also wine country, with some of the oldest wineries in the Middle East. Zahlé, the main town, is known for its riverside restaurants, where long lunches of mezze and grilled meats are served with arak, an aniseed spirit diluted with water.

Travel in Lebanon needs careful thought. The country has faced conflict, economic crisis and instability, and the Bekaa in particular has seen security incidents and airstrikes in recent years. Check current government advice before planning a trip. If conditions allow, the ride from Beirut over Mount Lebanon to the Bekaa is spectacular, climbing to a high pass with views back over the Mediterranean, though snow can close the road in winter and traffic is chaotic.

Zahlé, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of mezze, with hummus, tabbouleh and kibbeh, and fresh trout by the springs of Aanjar.
t.forest of the cedars@34.2,36.0:
High in the mountains of northern Lebanon, at close to two thousand metres above the Qadisha valley, a small grove of ancient cedars survives as a reminder of the vast forests that once covered these slopes. The Phoenicians built their ships from cedar, the Egyptians used its resin, and the Bible says that Solomon's temple was built with it. Over thousands of years, the forests were cut down almost entirely, and the Cedars of God, as this grove is called, is one of the last remnants, with some trees thought to be many centuries old. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Ouadi Qadisha, the Holy Valley, and the Forest of the Cedars of God.

The Qadisha valley below is a deep gorge carved into the limestone, home since the early Middle Ages to monasteries, hermitages and caves used by Maronite Christians seeking refuge and solitude. The town of Bsharri, perched on the edge of the gorge, is the birthplace of the poet Khalil Gibran, author of The Prophet, and his museum, in an old monastery, holds his paintings and his tomb. In winter, The Cedars becomes a ski resort, one of the oldest in the Middle East.

The road to the cedars is a spectacular ride: from Tripoli on the coast, it climbs through olive groves and villages, then up a series of hairpins along the edge of the Qadisha valley, with dizzying drops and incredible views. The surface is variable, with potholes, gravel and the occasional rockfall, and local drivers can be unpredictable. In winter, snow often closes the upper road. Spring, when the snow is melting and the valleys are green, and autumn are the best times.

Before any trip, check current travel advice, as the security situation in Lebanon can change quickly. Bsharri, four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try mezze, a spread of small dishes such as hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh and grilled meats, with fresh bread. A cup of strong Lebanese coffee, flavoured with cardamom, will warm you up at altitude, where the air is cool even in summer.
t.qalaat chakra@33.2,35.5:
Before anything else, the honest part: this place lies in southern Lebanon, a few kilometres from the border with Israel, in an area that has seen repeated war, most recently in 2024, and that remains militarised and unpredictable. The listed neighbours on the route sheet, from Kiryat Shmona to Tyre, sit on opposite sides of a frontier that is closed to ordinary travel. Check your government's travel advice and local conditions very carefully before even thinking about a visit, and do not try to approach from the Israeli side.

The fortress near the village of Chakra, in the hills of Jabal Amel, is one of a chain of hilltop castles that dotted this region from the Crusader period onward. Fortifications like this one guarded the routes between the coast at Tyre and the upper Jordan valley, changing hands between Crusaders, Ayyubids, Mamluks and local lords over the centuries, and later being reused and rebuilt. Their stone walls, set on limestone ridges among olive groves and scrub oak, give wide views over the rolling hills and wadis toward Galilee.

The landscape is beautiful in a quiet, rural way: terraced hillsides with olives and tobacco, small villages of stone houses, oak and pine woods and deep valleys carved by seasonal streams. The light in spring, after the winter rains, is soft and green, and the smell of wild thyme and sage fills the air. Summer is hot and dry.

When the situation allows, riding in southern Lebanon means narrow, winding roads through hill villages, with variable surfaces, frequent checkpoints, unpredictable traffic and plenty of military presence. Fuel is available in the larger villages and towns, and Tyre, on the coast, is the main city of the south, with everything a traveller needs. Tyre itself is a UNESCO site, with spectacular Roman and Byzantine remains, a hippodrome and colonnaded streets by the sea, and a lively fishing harbour.

Local food is delicious: mezze of hummus, tabbouleh and fresh bread, grilled meats, olive oil and local cheese, and strong coffee scented with cardamom. Hospitality here is warm, often overwhelming. But this is a place where the news decides whether you ride, not the weather or the season. Read the latest reports, listen to local advice, and accept that some routes are better saved for another year.
t.old city of jerusalem and its walls@31.8:
Few square kilometres on earth carry as much weight as these. The Old City of Jerusalem holds sites sacred to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, packed into a maze of stone lanes inside walls built by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in the 1530s. The Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Dome of the Rock and the al-Aqsa Mosque lie within a few minutes' walk of each other, and the city's four traditional quarters, Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian, each have their own character, markets and rhythms. The Old City and its walls were added to the UNESCO list in 1981.

Walking the walls is one of the best ways to understand the city: a rampart path runs along much of the circuit, with views into courtyards, rooftops and domes on one side and the modern city on the other. The gates, from Jaffa Gate to Damascus Gate and the Lions' Gate, each have their own story and atmosphere. Inside, the alleys are full of shops, spice stalls, bakeries and pilgrims from every corner of the world.

This is not a place to ride into. The Old City is pedestrian, with steep stone steps and narrow lanes, and the streets around it are congested, with heavy traffic, buses, taxis and limited parking. Leave the bike in a secure car park outside the walls and explore on foot. Riding to Jerusalem from the coast or the Dead Sea is spectacular, though: the road from the Dead Sea climbs more than a thousand metres through the Judean desert, a dramatic ascent through bare hills and canyons.

Fuel, food and lodging are everywhere in the city. Food is a highlight: hummus in small family restaurants, fresh falafel, sesame bread rings called ka'ak, knafeh soaked in syrup, and fresh juice squeezed in front of you. Dress modestly when visiting religious sites, and be aware of prayer times, holidays and closures.

Jerusalem is a city of strong emotions and real tensions, and security conditions can change quickly. Check current advice before visiting, follow local guidance and be respectful of the many communities who live and worship here. Come early in the morning, when the light is golden on the stone and the lanes are quiet, and listen to the bells and calls to prayer echoing over the rooftops.
t.ouadi qadisha@34.3,36.0:
Cliffs fall hundreds of metres into the Qadisha valley in northern Lebanon, and halfway down, tucked into caves and ledges, are monasteries and hermitages where Maronite Christians have prayed and hidden for over a thousand years. The name means holy, and the valley was a refuge for monks and believers fleeing persecution. The monastery of Qannoubine, seat of the Maronite patriarchs for centuries, clings to the rock, and the monastery of Saint Anthony of Qozhaya kept one of the first printing presses in the Middle East, used to print psalms in Syriac. UNESCO lists the valley together with the forest of the Cedars of God above it.

Bsharri, the main town, sits on the rim of the valley, a cluster of stone houses with red roofs. It is the birthplace of Khalil Gibran, the poet of The Prophet, and his museum and tomb are in a former hermitage on the edge of town. Above Bsharri, at about two thousand metres, the Cedars of God are a small grove of ancient trees, some of them very old, the last remnants of the forests that once covered the mountains of Lebanon and provided wood for Phoenician ships and Solomon's temple.

The riding here is spectacular. The road up from Tripoli or the coast climbs steeply through villages and terraces, with tight hairpins, narrow sections and views down into the valley. The surface varies from good to broken, and local drivers can be unpredictable. In winter, snow closes the high roads around the cedars, and fog is common. Summer is the best season, with warm days and cool nights. The roads into the valley itself are narrow and steep, and many monasteries can only be reached on foot.

Bsharri has pumps, a supermarket and a few places to eat; Tripoli, on the coast, is the nearest large city. Lebanese food is a feast: mezze of hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh and grilled meats, fresh bread and local wine and arak. Before you travel, check the current security situation and the advice of your government, as conditions in Lebanon can change fast. If you go, walk at least part of the way into the valley, past the hermitages and down to the river, and listen to the silence that drew the monks here centuries ago.
t.masada@31.3,35.4:
The Dead Sea lies more than four hundred metres below sea level, the lowest point on land, and Masada rises above its western shore as a vast flat-topped rock with sheer cliffs on every side. King Herod built a palace fortress here in the first century BC, with storerooms, cisterns, bathhouses and a three-tiered palace hanging from the northern cliff. After the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem in AD 70, a group of Jewish rebels held out on the rock against the Roman army. The Romans built a siege ramp up the western side, and according to the historian Josephus, when the walls were breached, the defenders chose to die rather than be captured.

The remains of the Roman siege camps and the ramp are still visible around the base of the rock, and from the top you can see them laid out like a diagram. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage list. A cable car takes visitors to the summit from the eastern side, by the Dead Sea, and the Snake Path climbs the same face on foot, best done before dawn to watch the sun rise over the mountains of Jordan.

The riding is extraordinary. Route 90 runs along the shore of the Dead Sea, through a landscape of white salt, brown cliffs and blue water, with heat haze shimmering on the road. The road from Arad descends from the plateau to the western side of Masada, with spectacular views and tight bends, and there is a separate access to the base of the Roman ramp. Summer heat is fierce, often over forty degrees, so ride early and carry water. Winter is pleasant and sunny. Watch for sand on the road and sudden flash floods after rare rainstorms.

The hotels at Ein Bokek, on the Dead Sea shore, have shops and restaurants, and Arad, on the plateau, has fuel and services. Israeli food here means hummus, salads and grilled meats, with fresh juice to fight the heat. Before you travel, look at recent travel advice. Visit the summit early, wander through Herod's storerooms and palaces, and stand at the edge of the cliff looking down at the Roman camps. Then ride down to the Dead Sea and float in the salty water, an unforgettable experience.
t.persian quarter@32.8,35.0:
Haifa climbs the northern slope of Mount Carmel in tiers, and halfway up, a golden dome catches the light above a staircase of gardens that tumbles all the way down to the old German Colony and the port. This is the Bahá'í World Centre, and the dome crowns the Shrine of the Báb, the founder figure of the Bahá'í faith, whose remains were brought here from Persia and interred on the mountainside. The nineteen terraces around it, with clipped lawns, gravel paths, cypresses and fountains, are among the most meticulously kept gardens anywhere, and together with the shrine of Bahá'u'lláh near Acre across the bay they form a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Persian connection runs through everything here, from the faith's origins in nineteenth-century Iran to the formal geometry of the planting.

Below the gardens, Ben Gurion Avenue runs straight down to the sea through the German Colony, founded in the 1860s by the Templers, a German Protestant sect who built solid stone houses with red tiled roofs and Bible verses carved over the doors. Many of those houses are now restaurants and cafés, and the avenue lines up with the terraces so precisely that standing at the bottom you see the whole composition stacked above you. Haifa as a whole is a working city, a port and an industrial centre with a mixed Jewish and Arab population, and it has a less frantic feel than Tel Aviv or Jerusalem.

Riding in Haifa itself is steep, busy and full of hairpins, as streets switchback up the mountain with parked cars on both sides and buses grinding along. The rewards are on the ridge: the road along the top of the Carmel runs through pine forest and Druze villages such as Daliyat al-Karmel, with views down to the coastal plain and, on a clear day, north toward the Lebanese border. The Carmel forest suffered a devastating fire in 2010, and you will still see its traces. Summer heat is intense, so the cool of early morning suits the mountain best.

Fuel, food and every service are easily found in Haifa. For a meal, the German Colony or the Wadi Nisnas neighbourhood offer hummus, grilled meat and Arab sweets. The gardens have strict rules on dress and behaviour, and the upper and lower terraces are reached on guided routes at set times, so check before you go. Then sit with a coffee at the bottom of the avenue and enjoy the view of a mountain wearing a crown.
t.qalaat al chakif@33.3,35.5:
Perched on a cliff edge some three hundred metres above the gorge of the Litani river in southern Lebanon, Beaufort Castle, known in Arabic as Qalaat al-Chakif, has watched over the borderlands of the Levant for nearly a thousand years. The Crusaders took and fortified it in the twelfth century, and it was finally surrendered to Saladin in 1190 after a long siege. Later it was held by the Mamluks, rebuilt and repaired by local rulers, and in the twentieth century it became a fiercely contested military position, occupied by Palestinian fighters and then by the Israeli army from 1982 until its withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000. Its stones have been battered by everything from siege engines to modern artillery.

The view from the top is the thing. To the east and south the land falls away into the Litani valley, and on a clear day you can see Mount Hermon, often snow-capped, and the hills of northern Israel and the Golan. The Litani itself cuts a deep, winding gorge here before turning west toward the sea near Tyre. The countryside is rocky and dry, scattered with olive and tobacco fields and small villages, and in spring the hills turn green with wildflowers for a few short weeks.

A word of honesty is needed. Southern Lebanon has been the scene of repeated conflict, including heavy fighting in recent years, and the border area near the castle has been directly affected. Before even thinking of riding here, check the current travel advice from your government, which may well advise against all travel to this region, and be prepared for military checkpoints and restrictions. If and when it is safe, the roads from Nabatieh climb through hilly country with tight bends and variable surfaces, and the approach to the castle offers dramatic views.

Nabatieh, a large town about eight kilometres away, is where fuel, food and services are found. The local food is southern Lebanese: grilled meats, fresh bread, mezze and strong coffee. When conditions allow a visit, give yourself time to walk around the ruins and stand at the cliff edge above the river, because few castles anywhere sit on such a site. For now, though, this is a place to read about and respect, and to visit only when peace returns.
t.qalaat deir kifa@33.3,35.4:
Southern Lebanon has a castle on almost every second hilltop, and Qalaat Deir Kifa is one of the less-known ones, a ruined fortification above the village of Deir Kifa in the rolling hills of Jabal Amel, between the Litani river and the coast at Tyre. Like many sites in this landscape, it has been built on, fought over and reused across several eras, and today what remains is stone walls, scattered blocks and a view across a countryside of olive groves, tobacco terraces and stony ridges.

Its better-known neighbour gives a sense of the region's history. A short distance to the east, the Crusader castle of Beaufort, Qalaat al-Shaqif, stands above the Litani gorge near Arnoun, one of the great medieval fortresses of the Levant. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries this was a contested frontier between Crusader lordships and Muslim states, and smaller forts and watchtowers like the one at Deir Kifa guarded roads and valleys between larger strongholds. The area's history runs much deeper, too: Tyre on the coast was one of the great Phoenician cities, and its Roman ruins and hippodrome are among the finest in the eastern Mediterranean.

On a map the riding looks appealing. Roads loop through the hills from Nabatieh toward Tyre and the coast, with constant changes of gradient, tight corners through villages and long views over valleys to Mount Hermon, white with snow in winter and spring. In practice, southern Lebanon has been a war zone in recent years, with heavy fighting along the border and in the villages throughout this area, and damage and unexploded ordnance are real risks. Anyone thinking of riding here must check current official travel advice first, stay on main roads, and be guided by local people about what is safe.

Practicalities depend on the situation at the time. Nabatieh, around fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel, food and shops in normal conditions, and Tyre has everything a traveller would need. Lebanese food is a pleasure anywhere: manakish from the bakery in the morning, a plate of hummus and grilled meat at midday, and strong coffee scented with cardamom.

If the time comes when the hills are calm again, this will be a beautiful corner to ride, with spring wildflowers on the terraces, the smell of thyme on the wind, and a castle wall to sit on while the sun goes down over the sea.
t.junayn garden@33.0,35.1:
On the coastal plain of western Galilee, between Nahariya and Akko, a small garden known as Junayn is one of the Bahá'í holy places in Israel. Bahá'u'lláh, the founder of the Bahá'í Faith, spent his final years in exile in this region in the late nineteenth century, after being banished by the Ottoman authorities from Persia and then from Baghdad, Istanbul and Edirne. Once his confinement in the prison-city of Akko was relaxed, he would visit gardens around the town, and this was one of them. The Bahá'í holy places in Haifa and western Galilee, including the Shrine of Bahá'u'lláh at Bahjí and the terraced gardens on Mount Carmel, were listed by UNESCO in 2008. The gardens are tended with remarkable precision by Bahá'í volunteers from around the world, and the atmosphere is serene.

The region is rich in history. Akko, a few kilometres south, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, a walled port that was the last stronghold of the Crusaders in the Holy Land until 1291. Its Crusader halls, Ottoman mosques, caravanserais and markets are a UNESCO site, and its fish restaurants by the harbour are excellent. Nahariya, to the north, is a coastal town founded in the 1930s by German Jewish immigrants, with a promenade and beaches. Further north, at Rosh HaNikra, white chalk cliffs plunge into the sea, with grottoes carved by the waves, reached by cable car.

The riding is coastal and relaxed. The main road runs along the coastal plain, flat and busy, through fields, orchards and towns. Inland, the roads climb into the hills of western Galilee, with villages, olive groves and pine forests, and the views over the sea are lovely. The surface is generally good, but traffic is dense and driving can be aggressive.

Nahariya and Akko have fuel, shops and restaurants. Spring, when the hills are green and covered with wildflowers, is the best season; summer is hot and humid. This area lies close to the Lebanese border, and the security situation in the region has been volatile, so check current travel advice carefully before planning a visit and follow local instructions.
t.umm al jimal@32.3,36.4:
Umm al-Jimāl is a black town in a yellow desert. Built almost entirely of dark basalt, it rises from the plain of northern Jordan, near the Syrian border, about fifteen kilometres east of Mafraq. People lived here for centuries, from the Nabataean period through Roman, Byzantine and early Islamic times, and what survives today is an extraordinary rural town of houses, churches, water reservoirs, barracks and streets, many buildings still standing two or three storeys high. Because wood was scarce, the builders used long basalt slabs to make floors and roofs, supported on corbels and arches, and some of the stairways leading to the upper floors still cling to the walls. In 2024 UNESCO listed the site, recognising it as an exceptional example of a farming and trading town on the edge of the desert.

The name means mother of camels, a reference to the caravans that once passed through. Wandering among the ruins, with the dark stones absorbing the heat and the silence broken only by birds and the wind, you get a powerful sense of daily life in a town that faded slowly rather than being destroyed. Look for the Latin and Greek inscriptions, the crosses carved on lintels of the churches, and the huge cisterns that collected the scarce winter rain.

The Hauran, the volcanic plateau that stretches north into Syria, is a landscape of black basalt boulders, wheat fields and scattered villages. Bosra, just across the Syrian border, has a Roman theatre of the same dark stone, but the frontier is not a place to approach casually. To the southeast, the desert castles of the Umayyads, such as Qusayr Amra with its frescoes, are within reach along the desert highway.

The roads are straight, wide and mostly empty outside the towns, with long sightlines across the plain. Watch for trucks heading to and from Iraq and Saudi Arabia, sheep and dogs, and sudden potholes and speed bumps in villages. Wind and dust can be strong, and the heat in summer is relentless. Come between October and April.

Mafraq, the nearest town, has fuel, shops and simple restaurants. Bring water, a hat and sunscreen, and accept any invitation to tea; Jordanian hospitality is legendary. Check the travel advice for areas near the Syrian border before you go.
t.old city of acre@32.9,35.1:
Acre has been a port for roughly four thousand years, but the city you walk through today is a layered one. Beneath the Ottoman streets lies the headquarters of the Crusader kingdom's last years, when Acre was the capital and a thriving trading harbour, with the Knights Hospitaller building a vast complex of vaulted halls that were buried and forgotten for centuries. In 1291 the Mamluks took the city, and with that the Crusader presence on the mainland ended. The tunnels and halls have been dug out and restored, and walking through the knights' halls is eerie and cool even in August.

The later city is the work of Ahmad al-Jazzar, the Ottoman governor of the late eighteenth century, whose mosque, citadel and walls dominate the old quarter. His defences held in 1799 against Napoleon, who besieged the town for two months before retreating, and the sea walls still look strong. The old harbour is small, with fishing boats and cafes, and the lanes behind it are noisy with the smell of coffee, spices and fresh fish.

Acre is a city of about forty-five thousand, so fuel, parking and food are easy, though the old town is partly pedestrian and the car parks near the gate fill quickly on weekends. Hummus is a local obsession, and you will find places arguing about who does it best. Eat it for breakfast, with warm bread, and walk off the lunch along the sea wall.

For riders, the region is varied. The coastal road north toward Rosh HaNikra gives you sea views, banana plantations and fast, easy riding, while roads inland climb into the hills of Western Galilee, with oak and pine woods, Arab and Druze villages and tight corners. Traffic can be heavy near Haifa and around the main junctions, and drivers are quick, so stay alert. Summers are hot and humid on the coast, so start early, and spring is the best season, when the hills are green and wildflowers are everywhere. Remember that many businesses close for the Jewish Sabbath from Friday afternoon, and the Arab quarters keep their own rhythm, so plan fuel and food around that.
t.ridvan gardens@32.9,35.1:
In the spring of 1863, Bahá'u'lláh, the founder of the Bahá'í faith, spent twelve days in a garden in Baghdad that Bahá'ís now call Ridván, the Garden of Paradise, and the festival of that name still marks the most holy days in their calendar. The garden outside Acre that carries the same name is a different place, a quiet green island on the Na'amán river, east of the old city, which Bahá'u'lláh loved during his years as a prisoner and exile of the Ottomans in Acre. He called it the New Jerusalem, and visitors who enter its small gate understand why. The river runs around it, mulberry trees give shade, and the air is cool and smells of water.

The garden belongs to the group of Bahá'í holy places in Haifa and Western Galilee, which UNESCO listed in 2008, along with the Shrine of Bahá'u'lláh at Bahjí a few kilometres north, and the terraced gardens of the Shrine of the Báb in Haifa. These are living places of pilgrimage, tended by volunteers, and the standard of care is high. Opening hours are limited and change, there are dress guidelines and no commercial activity, so check before you go, and keep a quiet voice.

For riders, getting here is simple. Acre is a city of about forty-five thousand people and has fuel, cafes and parking, and the garden is only a short way from the coast road. The roads around Acre and the Western Galilee are fast and busy, with plenty of roundabouts and local drivers who are quick to pull out, so keep a wide margin. If you want something more relaxed, ride inland past Judeida-Makr and into the hills, where narrow roads wind through olive groves, oak woods and small villages with warm bakeries.

The best time to go is spring, when the gardens are green and the weather mild, and the second best is autumn, after the heat breaks. Midsummer is humid and sticky near the sea, so go early. Make time for a sit by the water, and think of how long a garden can stay in people's minds.
t.qalaat tibnin@33.2,35.4:
Tibnin is a castle on a hill in south Lebanon, and the story it tells is one of rival crowns trading the same piece of ground. The Crusaders built it in the early twelfth century, around 1105, under Hugh of St Omer, and called it Toron. It sat between the coast at Tyre and the road to Damascus, and from its walls a garrison could see raiders coming a long way off. Saladin took it in 1187, and the fortress changed hands and shape for centuries afterwards, ending up a half-ruined hill crowned with pale stone, with a village of the same name spread around it.

The country around is green hill country, quite unlike the dry image many people have of Lebanon. Terraces of olive trees, tobacco fields, oaks and wild thyme roll away in every direction, with stone villages on the ridges, and on a clear day you can pick out the pale line of the sea and the dark shoulder of the Galilee hills across the border. Ain Ebel, a Christian village a short way south, is quiet and sleepy, and the road beyond runs toward the frontier.

That frontier matters. South Lebanon has seen repeated conflict, and the security situation changes from month to month, with checkpoints, closed roads and in some periods no safe access at all. Fuel and cash are best sorted in the larger towns, Nabatieh and Tyre among them, and the supply of petrol in Lebanon has been unreliable in recent years, so carry a margin and do not assume a village pump will be open.

When conditions allow, this is a very good ride. The roads are twisty and often narrow, with tight bends between walls, poor patches, loose gravel and the odd cow, and drivers are fast and relaxed about lanes. Go in spring, when the hills are bright with wildflowers and anemones, or in autumn after the heat. Summer afternoons are hot and hazy, and winter brings rain and fog to the higher slopes. Take a coffee from the village shops, and talk to people, because south Lebanon is generous with hospitality to anyone who arrives with respect.
t.mount amel castles@33.2,35.4:
It is a region of terraced slopes, olive groves, tobacco patches and stone villages, with the Hula valley falling away to the east and the long wall of Mount Hermon hanging over everything on a clear day. The nearest settlements are Ain Ebel on the Lebanese side and Qiryat Shemona and Metulla on the Israeli side, which tells you most of what you need to know about the place: this is a frontier, and the frontier shapes every road.

The castles in the label are the Crusader strongholds that once watched these ridges. Beaufort perched above the Litani gorge, Toron at Tibnin and Chastel Neuf at Hunin were all part of a chain built to hold the road between Damascus and the coast, and the same logic of high ground and long views is why the lanes here climb the way they do. The country between them is steep and twisty, with short, tight bends, rough patches of asphalt and sudden drops into dry wadis. Spring is the season to ride it, when the hillsides are green and the poppies are out; by August the slopes turn the colour of toast and the heat settles into the valleys.

I will be straight about the practical side. This is one of the most sensitive borders in the Middle East, and which roads are open, which are military zones and which you should not point a motorbike at changes with the news. Check current conditions and local advice before you plan anything here, and do not wander toward the fence for a photograph. On the Israeli side, Qiryat Shemona is a proper town of some twenty thousand people with fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Metulla, the little border village at the tip of the Galilee panhandle, is good for a coffee and a quiet look at the Lebanese hills across the valley.

If you are here for history, bring a map and some patience, because the stones are scattered and often fenced off. Arrive with a full tank from the larger town, carry water in summer, and treat the day as a slow wander through a landscape that has been fought over for a thousand years and still has not quite settled down.
t.north slope of mount carmel@32.8,35.0:
Haifa is the one big Israeli city where you really do ride up a mountain to get home. The north slope of Mount Carmel drops almost straight into the Mediterranean, and the city is stacked on it in layers: port and railway at the bottom, then the German Colony with its tidy Templer houses, then the long terraces of the Bahá'í Gardens, and finally the ridge, where the road along the top gives you the whole bay as far as Acre on a clear afternoon.

The gardens are the reason this stop has a place on a heritage route. Nineteen terraces climb the slope to the golden-domed Shrine of the Báb, which holds the remains of the forerunner of the Bahá'í faith, and the whole thing is kept so immaculately that it looks as if it was painted on rather than planted. You walk it in your boots and your jacket like everyone else, and the gardeners look at you with polite tolerance. Higher up on the headland sits the Stella Maris monastery, a Carmelite house that traces the order back to hermits who settled on this mountain in the twelfth century, and who took their name from it. The prophet Elijah is tied to the mountain in all three of the great faiths, which is why the cave beneath the monastery draws so many visitors.

The riding is city riding with a lot of altitude change. The roads that climb from the port, Hanassi Boulevard along the ridge and the switchbacks of Yefe Nof, are all steep and tightly curved, and in the afternoon they fill with buses, taxis and delivery vans. Early morning is far better, with cooler air and the light coming in low off the sea. Haifa has an underground funicular, the Carmelit, with six stops, and it is a small railway marvel if you are ever tempted to leave the bike for an hour.

Fuel is easy; there are stations throughout the city and in Tirat Karmel to the south. The Carmel itself is a limestone ridge covered with pine, oak and wild herbs, and the national park above the city has some of the best forest riding in the country, with the scent of resin and thyme after rain. The Druze villages of Daliyat al-Karmel and Isfiya sit along the crest and serve grilled meat, pita and strong coffee that will keep you upright for the descent.
t.palestine land of olives and vines cult@:
Battir is the quiet village at the heart of this cultural landscape, in the hills southwest of Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where terraces of dry stone climb the slopes in layer after layer. They are planted with olives, vines, and the vegetables that Battir is famous for, especially a small, sweet kind of aubergine. UNESCO inscribed the area in 2014 as the Land of Olives and Vines, a cultural landscape of southern Jerusalem, because the terraces, the irrigation channels and the old watch-towers show an agricultural system that has worked for many centuries.

The remarkable thing is the water. A spring called Ain al-Jama'in feeds a system of channels and pools, and for generations the water has been divided among the village families on a rota, each getting a set period at a set hour. Every pool and every channel has a place in the schedule, and elders can still say whose turn it is. It is a form of common management that has outlasted empires. A railway line built by the Ottomans in the 1890s, linking Jaffa and Jerusalem, also runs through the valley, adding a rusting counterpoint to the terraces.

The surrounding hills are a mix of limestone ridges, scrub and cultivated slopes, with fig, almond and pomegranate trees, and in spring the land is covered in wild flowers. The light in early morning and late afternoon turns the stone a pale gold. These roads are narrow, winding and often steep, passing small villages and with the occasional checkpoint, and conditions in the area can change quickly. Anyone planning to ride here should check the current situation, local advice and what is allowed on a foreign-plated vehicle, and keep documents close at hand.

Battir has just over four thousand people, and Husan nearby has more than five thousand, so you will find some small shops, cafes and fuel in the area, and Bethlehem, a few kilometres east, has more choices. Walking in the terraces is the best way to understand the place, and the old paths between the fields and the spring are open to the careful visitor. Spring, with green slopes, and autumn, when the olive harvest is on, are the best seasons. Summer is hot and dry, and winter can be wet and cold.
t.petra@30.3,35.4:
Petra is the most famous ruin in Jordan, and it earns the fame. The Nabataeans, an Arab people who grew rich on the incense and spice trade, carved their capital into the rose-coloured sandstone cliffs of a hidden valley more than two thousand years ago. You approach through the Siq, a narrow gorge about a kilometre long, with walls rising on either side until, at the end, the Treasury appears in a slice of light, a monumental facade cut straight out of the rock.

The city declined after the Romans annexed it in the early second century and after earthquakes and shifts in trade routes weakened it. For centuries it was known only to local Bedouin, until the Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812, disguised as a Muslim pilgrim. The poet John William Burgon later called it a rose-red city half as old as time. UNESCO listed the site in 1985, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.

You will probably ride in along the Kings Highway, the old route that runs along the plateau above the Rift Valley from Madaba and Karak in the north to Aqaba in the south. It is one of the great riding roads of the Middle East, with long curves, wide views and fields and villages along the way. Surfaces are generally good on the main route, though goats and slow trucks can appear around any corner, and the weather in winter can be cold with rain and sometimes snow on the high plateau.

The modern town of Wadi Musa lies at the gate of the site and has fuel stations, hotels, cafes and everything a traveller needs. Go into Petra early, because the heat builds fast and the site is huge. The walk to the Monastery is steep, with hundreds of rock-cut steps, but the view at the top is worth it. Take more water than you think you need, and wear shoes you can walk in.
t.bahji@32.9,35.1:
Acre is one of the oldest continuously inhabited ports in the world, and for the followers of the Bahá'í faith it has another meaning. Bahá'u'lláh, the founder, was exiled to the Ottoman prison city of Acre in 1868 and spent the rest of his life there, and in the countryside a few kilometres north of the walls he lived in a mansion called Bahjí. He died there in 1892, and the room in the house next door became a shrine. The shrine is the holiest place in the Bahá'í world, a quiet building of white stone with a glass-roofed courtyard, surrounded by gardens with lawns, hedges and palms. It was listed by UNESCO in 2008, with the Bahá'í sites in Haifa.

Visitors are welcome, and entry is free, but there are rules. Modest dress is expected, and shoes are taken off at the door of the inner room. Photography is not allowed in some areas, and the gardens are open at certain times, so check before you go. The atmosphere is peaceful, with the sound of fountains and the scent of orange blossom.

Acre itself is worth a few hours. The old city, built by the Crusaders and rebuilt by the Ottomans, is a maze of stone vaults, harbour walls and markets. The Hospitaller halls, under the street, are a very fine piece of medieval architecture, and the Al-Jazzar mosque, from the eighteenth century, has a lovely courtyard. Restaurants in the old port serve fresh fish and the local hummus, which is famously good.

The roads here are the coastal ones, the main highway running north and south and quieter lanes through the orchards of the Western Galilee. The surface is good and traffic is heavy at rush hours, with fast drivers and sudden stops. Rosh HaNikra, a set of sea caves near the Lebanese border, is a short ride north. Fuel is easy to find in Acre, a city of forty-five thousand people. The weather is hot in summer and humid, while spring and autumn are pleasant.

Conditions in this region can change, so check current advice about travel and access before you set out.
t.amman@32.0,35.9:
Amman is the starting point of Jordan's King's Highway, the old road that runs south through the country to the Red Sea, and it is also a city worth a day of its own. It is built on a series of hills, once seven, and the oldest part is the Citadel, which holds the pillars of a Roman temple to Hercules, a Byzantine church and an Umayyad palace, all on the same ridge. The ancient name was Philadelphia, after the Ptolemaic king who rebuilt it, and before that Rabbath Ammon, the capital of the Ammonites. Down in the valley below, a large Roman theatre, carved into the hillside and seating around six thousand people, still stages concerts.

Modern Amman is a young, fast-growing city of over a million people, many of them descended from refugees from Palestine, Iraq and Syria, and it has a lively, welcoming feel. Rainbow Street, with its cafes and old villas, is where people gather in the evening. The downtown souk, near the Roman theatre, is full of spice shops, sweet vendors and coffee sellers, and is the place to try knafeh, a hot cheese pastry soaked in syrup, and hummus with a drizzle of oil, served for breakfast.

Riding in the city is busy but manageable. Drivers are quick and often unpredictable, roundabouts are called circles and numbered, and hills are steep. The roads out are good. The King's Highway heads south through Madaba, famous for its mosaic map of the Holy Land, then down the Wadi Mujib canyon and on to Karak and Petra, with a series of long, winding sections through farmland and desert. It is slower than the fast Desert Highway but far more interesting. In summer the heat is fierce in the south, and in winter rain and even snow can fall on the high ground around Amman.

Fuel and workshops are everywhere, and the city has hotels at every price level. Evenings are cool, even in summer, because of the altitude of about nine hundred metres. Carry water on any journey, and keep your passport and papers accessible for the checkpoints on the main roads. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild days, and the hills around Amman turn green in early spring with a carpet of wildflowers.
t.crac des chevaliers@34.8,36.3:
T. E. Lawrence called Krak des Chevaliers the best preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world, and for once the praise is hardly exaggerated. It stands on a spur of the Jebel Ansariyeh in western Syria, controlling the Homs Gap, the low pass between the mountains and the sea through which armies and caravans have always passed. The Knights Hospitaller took it over in 1142, enlarged it into a concentric fortress of two rings of walls, and held it for over a century against repeated attacks. It could house a garrison of two thousand, with stables, storerooms, a great hall and a chapel, and the huge sloping glacis at the south side made the walls almost impossible to undermine.

Saladin looked at it in 1188 and decided not to attack. The Mamluk sultan Baybars took it in 1271, partly by a forged letter, it is said, ordering the garrison to surrender. After that it became a village, with people living inside the walls, until it was cleared in the 1930s and handed to the French authorities. The castle was listed by UNESCO in 2006 together with the nearby Qal'at Salah El-Din. The Syrian civil war damaged it, and it was held by rebel forces and shelled in 2013 before government forces recaptured it, so what stands today includes damage and repairs.

The security situation in Syria has been unstable for years, travel advice from most governments warns against visits, and borders, permits and road access change often. If you are reading this at a time when the country has opened to visitors, check current official advice first. The road from Homs towards the castle climbs from the plain through olive groves and orchards, with the walls appearing suddenly on the ridge, a view that has impressed every traveller since the Crusaders.

Tallkalakh, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel and basic shops. The setting is green and fertile in spring, with views across to Lebanon on a clear day. Local food includes kibbeh, grilled meat, sweet pastries and good olive oil. Weather in the hills can be cool and wet in winter, and the stone halls of the castle hold the cold, so bring a jacket even in autumn.
t.baha i holy places in haifa and the west:
Mount Carmel rises straight from the sea at Haifa, and on its northern slope a staircase of nineteen terraces of gardens, lawns and fountains climbs from the German Colony to the ridge, with the golden-domed Shrine of the Báb in the middle of it all. The Báb, a young merchant from Shiraz, proclaimed in 1844 that a new messenger of God would come, and he was executed in Tabriz in 1850. His remains were hidden and finally brought to Haifa and placed in a tomb on the slope, with the first building completed in 1909 and the present octagon with its dome of gold tiles finished in 1953. The terraces were completed in 2001. The gardens and the shrine, together with the sites at Bahji near Akko, make up the Baha'i Holy Places in Haifa and the Western Galilee, listed by UNESCO in 2008.

The gardens are among the most carefully kept in the world, with clipped hedges, lawn terraces, cypress trees and paths of pale stone, all tended by volunteers. From the upper terrace you look down a long axis of steps and flowerbeds to the German Colony and the sea, with Haifa's port and bay opening beyond. Visitors can walk through parts of the gardens free of charge, and guided tours go to the terraces and, at set hours, into the shrine, with respectful dress and quiet behaviour expected. Opening times and the arrangements for entry change, so check the official schedule.

Riding in Haifa means hills. The city climbs the side of Mount Carmel in steep streets and tight bends, with traffic to match, and the Carmelit, a small underground funicular, runs from the port to the top. Drive carefully on the Yefe Nof road along the ridge, which has views across the bay to Akko, and expect heavy rush-hour congestion. Parking near the lower gate is limited, and a motorcycle is easier to place than a car. The Mediterranean climate is hot and humid in summer, mild in winter, with rain between November and March.

Haifa has about a quarter of a million people, so fuel and services are plentiful. The German Colony, a street of Templer houses from the nineteenth century, is full of cafes and restaurants, and the nearby Wadi Nisnas quarter has Arab bakeries and falafel stalls. Try hummus and fresh pita for lunch, and a glass of lemon-and-mint cooler. Akko, about twenty-five kilometres north, has its Crusader harbour and is a fine day trip.
t.castrum@31.5,35.9:
Out on the plateau of central Jordan, east of the Dead Sea and south of Madaba, the land opens into a wide, treeless plain of wheat and barley, with low stone walls and the odd shepherd's tent. On that plain stand the ruins of Umm ar-Rasas, and the castrum is its oldest part, a rectangle of massive walls that began as a Roman military camp. It is probably of the late third or the fourth century, one of many forts that guarded the empire's edge against the desert tribes, and a garrison of auxiliary soldiers lived here. Its Roman name has been forgotten, and in the Byzantine age the town was called Kastron Mefaa. The walls still stand to a fair height, and inside is a jumble of collapsed houses, cisterns and arches, with a few churches among them.

After the Roman army withdrew, the camp became the core of a town, with churches built inside and around it, and later Muslim rulers left their own traces. The settlement continued through the early Islamic period and faded in the ninth century. Wandering through you find doorways with carved lintels, vaults half buried in sand and courtyards where pomegranate trees once grew, and the quiet is almost total. Nothing is roped off, but the stones are loose and the ground uneven, so take care.

This is high, open ground, about seven hundred metres or more above the sea, and the weather is often windy. Summer days are hot and dry, with a hazy light, and winter brings cold winds and occasional rain that turns the plain green. In spring the fields are carpeted with wild flowers, poppies and anemones among them, and storks and larks pass over. The best time to come is in the morning or the late afternoon, when long shadows pick out the details of the walls.

The roads are the real pleasure. From Madaba or from the King's Highway you take narrow, quiet tarmac across the plateau, with long views, gentle gradients and almost no traffic besides the occasional pickup and flock of sheep. Surfaces are generally fair, with patches of gravel at the edges. Signs can be sparse, so a map or a phone with offline maps helps. Fuel is not available at the site, and the small villages nearby may have a pump of doubtful supply, so fill up in Madaba, about twenty-eight kilometres away, and carry water and snacks.
t.area 1@32.5,36.5:
Bosra stands on the black basalt plain of the Hauran, in the south of Syria, close to the Jordanian frontier, and the whole town seems to be made of the dark volcanic stone that is found in the fields. It was a Nabataean town, and then the Romans made it the capital of the province of Arabia in the early second century, building a grid of streets, baths, a triumphal arch and one of the best-preserved theatres in the Roman world. The theatre could seat some fifteen thousand people. In the Middle Ages it was wrapped in a fortress by the Ayyubids, whose walls and towers rise around the stage, so that you can walk through the vaults beneath the seats and the old defences at the same time.

Bosra stood on the pilgrim and trade routes to Mecca and Damascus, and later it was a place of pilgrimage itself. A monastery, according to tradition, was the home of the monk Bahira, who recognised the young Muhammad as a future prophet when his uncle's caravan stopped here. The town has some of the earliest mosques in Syria, including the Mosque of Omar, with columns reused from Roman buildings. Many of the houses are old, and families lived among the ruins for centuries, with wells, cisterns and small shops. It was listed by UNESCO in 1980.

The label places it on a ride that passes the desert castle region, and the names in the area are mixed up, but the real place is Bosra. Look for current advice from official sources, and be prepared for the answer to be that you cannot go.

When access is possible, the surrounding plain is open farmland, with wheat, olive groves and stone-walled fields, and the roads run straight through the black rock country. The Hauran villages are built of basalt, and the doorways and lintels are often carved. Busra ash-Sham is a small town close to the ruins, and larger towns lie further away, so fuel is an issue to plan. The heat in summer is fierce, with winds from the desert, and the best seasons are spring and autumn.
t.um er rasas@31.5,35.9:
The most surprising thing at Umm ar-Rasas is a tower. It stands alone in the fields about a kilometre north of the old town, a tall square column of stone, about fifteen metres high, with no door and a small chamber at the top, and it was built for a stylite, one of those early Christian ascetics who lived on top of pillars to be closer to heaven and further from the world. Stylites became famous in Syria in the fifth century, and this tower, which dates from the Byzantine period, is one of very few that survive in the region, and it may have been used as late as the ninth century. A monk lived in that little room, and pilgrims came to see him.

The second surprise is the floor of the Church of Saint Stephen, in the old town. It is a mosaic, laid in the year 785 according to an inscription, and it shows a map of cities of the region, including Jerusalem, Nablus, Gaza, Philadelphia and the towns of the Nile Delta, each drawn as a walled town with towers and gates, in tiny coloured stones. Around them are hunting scenes, fish and birds. It is a rare thing: Christian art made under Muslim rule, in a time when some images were being defaced, and in places you can see where faces were erased. The mosaic is protected under a roof and has been conserved, and the site was listed by UNESCO in 2004.

Both are reached by quiet roads across the plateau, between the King's Highway and the edge of the desert. You pass fields of wheat and barley, goat herds and low villages, and the countryside has a bare, open beauty. The surface is mostly good tarmac, but patches are broken, and a strong crosswind often blows. Signs may be limited, so go prepared with a map. The ruins are open and usually uncrowded, with a small ticket office, and a caretaker will unlock the church if needed.

Bring water, and sun protection for the walk across the ruins. Spring is the loveliest season, when the plain is green and the wind is soft, and autumn is also pleasant. In winter, nights are cold and rain can turn the tracks to mud.
t.dana@30.6,35.6:
Dana is a village that clings to the edge of a cliff, and from its terrace the land falls away in a great gulf of rock, with the desert plain of Wadi Araba shimmering far below. It stands in the highlands of southern Jordan at about 1,200 metres, a cluster of old stone houses that were abandoned in the twentieth century and are now partly restored, at the heart of the Dana Biosphere Reserve, the largest nature reserve in the country.

The reserve covers a drop from high juniper hills to hot desert valleys, and this range of elevations gives it a rare mix of habitats. Wildlife includes ibex, red fox, and several rare birds, and the reserve has been a model for community-run conservation, with local families running guesthouses, a candle workshop and silversmithing. Hiking trails run down the wadi toward Feynan, where ancient copper mines show how long people have worked this land.

The road that brings you here is the Kings Highway, an ancient route that runs the length of Jordan along the top of the escarpment. In places it follows the line of the old Roman road, the Via Nova Traiana, built under Trajan, and earlier it was a caravan route mentioned in the Bible. Today it is a winding road with long views, passing castles, mosaics and small towns. It is generally well surfaced but slow in places, with trucks, sheep and speed bumps. Wind and chill can surprise, as the plateau is high, and it can snow in winter. Spring and autumn are best.

Dana is small and has limited services, so fill up at a larger town. Aţ Ţafīlah, about twenty-three kilometres away, is a good choice, and Buşayrā, closer, may have basic supplies. Locals will offer sweet tea and cardamom coffee, and the village guesthouses serve simple meals of flatbread, hummus and lentil soup. Bring warm clothing for evenings, since the air gets cold after dark.
t.miami@25.8,-80.2:
The Tamiami Trail was named for what it joined, Tampa and Miami, and it took thirteen years and an astonishing amount of dynamite to build. Begun in 1915 and opened in 1928, US 41 cuts straight west across the Everglades, one of the largest wetlands in North America, and it changed Florida by linking the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, though it also interrupted the flow of water across the Everglades in a way that scientists are still trying to repair. The road starts in downtown Miami as Southwest 8th Street, known to locals as Calle Ocho, the heart of Little Havana.

Miami is the most Latin of large American cities, and that is very much the point. In Little Havana, men play dominoes in the park, cafés serve cafecito, a tiny cup of very sweet, strong espresso, through street windows, and cigars are rolled by hand. Downtown has glass towers along Biscayne Bay, and nearby Vizcaya, an Italian-style villa of the early twentieth century, is a quiet retreat with gardens running down to the water. The city is hot and humid for most of the year, with sudden afternoon thunderstorms in summer and a hurricane season from June to November.

Leaving town on the Trail is a sudden change. Within half an hour, the suburbs fall away and the road runs straight through a wide flat landscape of sawgrass, canals and cypress, with white herons and alligators visible beside the road. Airboat operators offer rides, the Miccosukee tribe runs a cultural centre and the small post office at Ochopee claims to be the smallest in the country. Shark Valley, in Everglades National Park, has a tower with a view across the grass. The road is flat and monotonous, with a modest speed limit and plenty of police, and traffic can be heavy at weekends.

Fuel is easy in Miami but sparse in the Everglades section, with only a few stations, so fill up before leaving. Mosquitoes are ferocious from May to October, and so is the heat. The dry season, from December to April, is far more comfortable. Carry water and sunscreen, and keep a safe distance from alligators.
t.wadi mujib@31.5,35.6:
Wadi Mujib is a deep gorge in the Jordanian plateau, cut by the Mujib river on its way to the Dead Sea. The King's Highway crosses it on a dramatic descent, dropping from the high farmland of Moab down into the canyon and climbing out again on the far side, and the change of altitude is striking. The gorge is about four kilometres wide at the top and the floor lies close to the level of the Dead Sea, one of the lowest places on Earth. In the Bible this canyon was known as the Arnon, and it marked the border of Moab.

The riding is memorable rather than technical. The road swings down in long bends and hairpins, with views across the red, orange and ochre rock layers, and then climbs back up in the same way. Traffic includes trucks and tourist buses, so overtaking needs care, and the surface can be patchy after winter rain. Wind can be strong on the exposed sides. Heat is the main issue in summer, and the descent into the canyon feels like entering an oven.

Wadi Mujib is also a nature reserve, the lowest in the world, and its sandstone canyon holds a permanent river fed by springs and side streams. Ibex live in the cliffs, and the reserve has a good variety of birds and plants. Visitors can walk or wade in the water-filled gorge in season, with a guide and a permit from the reserve, but the river can flood suddenly after rain upstream, so it is not a place to wander without information.

There are no towns right at the gorge, so fuel and food are a matter of planning. The nearest sizeable town is Karak, known for its Crusader castle, about thirty kilometres south. Smaller villages like Ar Rabbah and Al Qasr are nearer but have limited services. Fill the tank before descending, carry water, and bring sun protection.

Stop at the viewpoint above the dam if you can. The scale of the canyon, and the thin line of road clinging to its walls, is easier to appreciate from a distance than from the saddle.
t.wadi mujib@31.5,35.8:
Wadi Mujib is the lowest nature reserve on Earth, and the Kings Highway crosses it in one of the most dramatic descents in Jordan. The road drops from the plateau near Madaba down the side of a great canyon, in a long series of bends, to a bridge at the bottom, and then climbs the other side, a change of several hundred metres in a few kilometres. The canyon, which the Bible calls the Arnon, was the boundary between the kingdoms of Moab and the Amorites, and it carves a deep red-brown gash through the sandstone toward the Dead Sea.

The Mujib river runs year-round, flowing out through a narrow gorge into the Dead Sea, whose shore lies around 430 metres below sea level, the lowest land on Earth and falling still. The reserve, run by Jordan's nature society, protects a remarkable range of habitats, from desert slopes to palm-lined pools, and is home to Nubian ibex, hyrax, foxes and many birds. The walking trails through the water-filled gorge are famous, but they are strictly managed, closed in the wet season when flash floods can kill, and need booking in advance.

The riding here is a joy. The Kings Highway is an old route, mentioned in the Book of Numbers, and the modern road follows it along the edge of the plateau, with wide views, tight hairpins and little traffic. The surface is generally good, but there can be sand, gravel and the occasional goat on the road, and the wind is strong on the exposed sections. Heat is the main issue: summer temperatures at the bottom of the gorge can exceed forty degrees, so carry plenty of water and wear ventilated gear. Spring and autumn are far kinder.

Dhiban, on the plateau to the south, is where in the nineteenth century a black basalt stone was found bearing an inscription by Mesha, king of Moab, the earliest known text to mention the God of Israel outside the Bible. Fuel is a practical concern: the nearest big town is Madaba, twenty-eight kilometres away, and a few small stations lie on the road, so fill up before the descent. Simple cafes by the roadside serve strong tea and fresh bread. The best seasons are March to May and October to November, when the light on the canyon walls is glorious.
t.ancient city of bosra@32.5,36.5:
Bosra rises out of a plain of black volcanic rock in the south of Syria, near the Jordanian border, and everything in it is built of basalt: the Roman theatre, the Nabataean-era streets, the mosques and the houses that people still lived in. It was the capital of the Roman province of Arabia, and later a major stop on the caravan routes between Damascus and the Arabian Peninsula. UNESCO listed the ancient city in 1980.

The theatre is the astonishment. Dating from the second century AD, it seats around fifteen thousand people and survives with its stage building largely intact, because in the Middle Ages it was turned into a fortress, with towers added around it, and that protected it from being quarried. Nearby is the Mosque of Omar, said to be one of the oldest in the Islamic world, and the Cathedral ruins that tell of the city's Christian centuries. Tradition holds that the young Muhammad met the monk Bahira here on a caravan journey, though historians treat the story with care.

Riding in is flat and open, through the Hauran plain, a granary of wheat and barley since Roman times, with dark stone walls dividing the fields. The road surfaces vary and the sun in summer is fierce, so mornings are far better. Spring turns the plain green and sprinkles it with red poppies, while in winter the wind from the east is cold. Sabha, the nearest larger town, and the villages around Bosra offer basic services.

Be realistic about the situation: Syria has been through years of conflict, and Bosra was damaged in the fighting. Conditions, access and safety have changed over time, so any rider thinking of this region should check current official advice carefully before planning a visit. If you do go, or if you are following the story from afar, the lesson of the place is the same: a city that survived Rome, Byzantium, the Crusades and earthquakes has more resilience than most.
t.area 2@32.5,36.5:
This is the Hauran, the volcanic plateau of southern Syria, where black basalt lies across the land like spilled coal and the villages are built of the same stone, so that houses seem to grow from the fields. Bosra, the famous Roman city, lies less than a kilometre from the spot, and everything around it follows the same dark theme.

The soil is the secret. Lava flows from the volcanic field to the east, which rises to the Jabal al-Druze mountain, broke down over millennia into deep, red-brown earth that grows excellent wheat.
