The Romans valued the region as a granary, and farmers still plough stony fields, stack the boulders into walls and plant olives and fruit trees where the ground allows. In spring the contrast of green shoots against black stone is unusually striking, and the sky is huge.

For motorcyclists, the terrain means long, straight roads across open plateau, with the occasional gentle bend around a wadi or old lava hill. Crosswinds can be strong, dust blows in summer, and the heat between June and September is severe, so start at dawn. Fuel and supplies are best taken in larger towns, since smaller villages have limited services, and the distances between settlements encourage careful planning. Sabha and Daraa lie in the surrounding area.

The area has been touched by conflict in recent years, and anyone drawn by the region's archaeology should consult up-to-date travel advice before making plans. Beyond that, it is worth knowing that the ride's other stop, Umm ar-Rasas, lies across the border in Jordan, with its mosaics and the tall stylite tower, evidence of the way this whole basalt country once formed a single cultural landscape linked by trade, faith and the road that led to Damascus. It is a landscape to understand slowly.
t.ouadi qadisha@34.3,37.0:
Two places are tangled in this label, and it helps to separate them. The Qadisha Valley, whose name means Holy Valley, is a deep gorge in northern Lebanon beneath the Cedars of God, where Maronite Christians settled in caves and built monasteries and hermitages from the early centuries. UNESCO inscribed it in 1998, and the cliffs there fall nearly straight into a river valley that ties together prayer, farming and defence.

That is a different country of stone, scrub and wind. The Qalamoun mountains run along this side of the Syrian interior, dry and pale, with villages in folds of limestone and orchards where water allows. Qara itself is a town of about twenty thousand people and the area has a long Christian and Muslim history. Nearby, the monastery of Mar Musa clings to a cliff, an ancient hermitage revived in modern times as a place of dialogue, though its situation has been affected by the region's conflicts.

Riding in this part of Syria is high desert: long straight sections on the main highway, crosswinds, hot dust in summer and cold nights on the plateau in winter. Surface quality varies and military checkpoints have been common in recent years, so a rider would need to be careful and well informed. Fuel is available in the larger towns on the main road, though supply has been disrupted at times, and water and shade are worth carrying.

If the Qadisha Valley is the goal, the better approach is from the Lebanese side, through Tripoli and Bsharri, birthplace of the poet Kahlil Gibran, whose museum sits in a monastery above the gorge. The road climbs steeply and the cedars sit higher still, ancient trees that provided the timber for Phoenician ships and, according to the Bible, for Solomon's temple. Check current travel advice for both countries before planning any trip, since conditions change.
t.key largo@25.1,-80.4:
Key Largo is the first of the Florida Keys, the one you reach after the long straight run down from Florida City, and it is also the biggest, stretching some thirty miles along the line of the old coral reef. The Overseas Highway, US 1, runs through its entire length, lined with dive shops, tackle stores, seafood shacks and motels. The town itself has about ten thousand people, and fuel, groceries and food are easy to find all along the road, which is marked by mile markers counted from Key West.

The island's name, Cayo Largo, means long key in Spanish, and its fame in popular culture comes from the 1948 film starring Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall, though most of it was shot on a Hollywood set. The African Queen, the little steamboat from the film of the same name, is on display in town. More important is John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, the first underwater park in the United States, established in 1960, which protects a long stretch of living reef where visitors snorkel and dive among parrotfish, barracuda and brain coral.

Riding here is straight and sunny, with the sea on both sides and the horizon flat. Speed limits are low, police are active, and the road is crowded with tourists in rental cars, so it is a ride of patience. The pleasure comes in the light and the colour, the turquoise of the shallows, the mangroves, and the sudden bridges. Wind can be strong, and afternoon thunderstorms in summer are sudden and heavy. A mosquito-proof evening is not guaranteed, particularly near the mangroves.

If you have the time, take the Card Sound Road, the older alternative route from the mainland, which runs through mangrove swamp and ends at a cheerfully weathered seafood restaurant and a toll bridge. Crocodiles live in the canals here, and the Everglades lie just to the west. The best months are December to April, with dry air and mild weather. Summer is hot and humid, and hurricane season runs to November. Book accommodation ahead for winter weekends, since the whole island fills up.
t.everglades national park@25.6,-81.0:
You will not see much on a map that tells you where you are, because the Everglades are a river wider than most counties and only a few inches deep. Marjory Stoneman Douglas called it the River of Grass in 1947, the year the park was dedicated, and the description holds: water flows slowly south from Lake Okeechobee across a sea of sawgrass toward Florida Bay, with islands of hardwood and pine rising a few feet above the flood.

The main road in, from Homestead and Florida City, runs about thirty-eight miles to Flamingo on the southern coast. It is flat, straight and quiet, and what makes it special is what you see beside it: alligators sunning on the banks of canals, anhingas drying their wings on branches, wood storks, ibises, and in the right season, spoonbills in pink flocks. The boardwalks at Anhinga Trail and Pa-hay-okee are short and easy, and the light at dawn is gorgeous. Alligators hold the road verges in the dry season, and they are best watched from a safe distance.

Timing matters. The wet season, from May to October, brings heat, afternoon storms and billions of mosquitoes, so riding in a hot jacket is a trial. From December to April it is dry and mild, the animals gather at the remaining water, and this is the time to go. Hurricanes come in late summer and autumn and can close the park.

Fuel is a plain matter: there is none on the road in, so fill up in Florida City or Homestead, which have plenty of stations and cheap motels. Services at Flamingo are limited. Take water, sun protection and insect repellent, because the park is a long way from anywhere. An entrance fee covers a week. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a wetland of international importance, and the sense of space, with sky and grass meeting at the horizon, is unlike anything else in the country.
t.mount nebo@31.8,35.7:
Mount Nebo is a modest ridge, a little over 800 metres high, in the hills above the Dead Sea in Jordan, but it has one of the most famous viewpoints in the Middle East. According to the Bible, this is the place where Moses was shown the Promised Land, before he died without crossing the Jordan. From the terrace, the land falls away dramatically, and on a clear day you can see the Jordan Valley, the northern end of the Dead Sea, the oasis of Jericho, and, in good light, the hills around Jerusalem. The haze often hides the farthest views, so the morning and late afternoon are best.

A Franciscan monastery stands on the summit, with a modern memorial church that houses the Byzantine mosaics of an earlier basilica, remarkable floors of hunting scenes, animals and trees in rich colours from the sixth century. A large twisted bronze serpent sculpture on the terrace recalls the story of Moses, and the whole place has a quiet, contemplative air, though tour buses can make it busy in the middle of the day.

The nearest town is Madaba, about nine kilometres away, with more than eighty thousand people, and it makes a good base. Its great treasure is the sixth-century mosaic map of the Holy Land on the floor of the Greek Orthodox church of Saint George, which shows Jerusalem and many other places in tiny coloured stones. Madaba has plenty of petrol stations, restaurants and shops, so fill up there before you start the long descent toward the Dead Sea.

The road up to Nebo is short, steep and winding, with good tarmac and wide views, and it takes you through olive groves and small farms. Traffic is heavier near the town and around the main tourist season, which runs from spring to autumn. In summer it can be very hot, with strong sun, so carry water and sun protection. In winter the weather is cooler, and occasional rain or fog can reduce the views.

Look out for the local bread, hummus and olive oil in Madaba. A cup of sweet tea with the view over the valley is the best way to end the visit.
t.dead sea@31.6,35.5:
The Dead Sea is the lowest point on the surface of the Earth, about 430 metres below sea level, and it is a strange experience to ride down to it. From Amman the road drops through the hills, with the temperature rising noticeably, until the great expanse of pale blue water appears beneath dry, ochre-coloured cliffs. The salt content is almost ten times that of the ocean, so nothing lives in it, and swimmers float effortlessly on the surface, reading a newspaper if they wish.

Today, with so much water taken for irrigation upstream, the sea is shrinking by roughly a metre a year, leaving white salt crusts and sinkholes along the shore. The scale of the change is visible in the old resort jetties that now stand far from the water. The lake is shared between Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, and the Jordanian side is reached by a smooth, well-kept highway that runs along the east shore.

The riding is pleasant, with long, gentle bends and views across to the Judean hills, though the heat is intense in summer, and the road can be busy with tour buses and lorries. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm sun and comfortable temperatures. Carry plenty of water, wear sun protection, and don't underestimate the strong light and the dry air.

If you swim, or rather float, follow the rules: do not splash, keep water away from your eyes, do not shave beforehand, and rinse in the fresh water showers afterwards. The mud on the shore is said to be good for the skin, and many people cover themselves in it. Hot springs, such as those at Ma'in, are found in canyons nearby.

Fuel stations along the shore road are spaced out, so fill the tank in Madaba or Amman before descending. There are resort hotels with day-pass beaches where you can leave your bike and gear safely, and have a meal, which is by far the easiest way to enjoy a float.
t.sault ste marie@46.5,-84.3:
Sault Ste. Marie sits on the St. Marys River, the short, fast channel that links Lake Superior to Lake Huron, and the city exists because the water here drops about seven metres over a set of rapids. The Ojibwe called the place Bawating, the place of the rapids, and it was a fishing and gathering ground long before French fur traders arrived in the seventeenth century. The name Sault, pronounced Soo, is the old French word for rapids. A twin city of the same name faces it across the river in Michigan, joined by the International Bridge, and the two are bound together by locks, trade and history.

The Canadian side is the start of one of the great northern drives. Highway 17 climbs away from town through hardwood forest and then follows the Lake Superior shore for hundreds of kilometres, past the cliffs and sandy bays of Lake Superior Provincial Park, with its ancient painted rock at Agawa, and on toward Wawa, home of a giant steel goose, and Marathon. The road is paved and mostly well kept, with long, undulating curves and good views of the lake, and it is known for rock cuts, lake mists and slowly changing light. The Algoma Central Railway, which runs inland from the Soo into the Agawa Canyon, is another local attraction, with autumn colour tours in September and early October.

Practical advice matters here, because the distances are big. Towns north of the Soo are widely spaced, with Wawa and White River the main fuel stops on the long middle stretch, and some stations close early. Moose and deer are common on the road, particularly at dusk. Weather on the lake can be abrupt, with fog, rain and a sharp drop in temperature, even in July. Carry rain gear, and do not count on a mobile signal in the gaps between towns.

Sault Ste. Marie itself has more than sixty thousand people, with all the services you might need, and a steel mill that has been central to its economy for over a century. The waterfront boardwalk and the old lock make a pleasant place to wander before the long ride north.

Finish a day here with whitefish from the lake, and a view of the lights across the river.
t.flagler beach@29.5,-81.1:
Flagler Beach is what much of the Florida coast used to be like. The little town stretches along a narrow barrier island between the Atlantic and the Intracoastal Waterway, with a long, broad beach of hard-packed sand, low buildings, a pier and a laid-back, unhurried feel that the high-rise resorts to the south left behind long ago. The population is about five thousand, and it is a place where people still walk to the beach, fish from the pier and eat at small seafood restaurants. State Road A1A, the coastal highway, runs right along the shore, with the sea on one side and the town on the other, and it is one of the most relaxed roads in the state.

The county and the town are named for Henry Flagler, the oil magnate who built the Florida East Coast Railway down the peninsula in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and who developed the great hotels of St Augustine and Palm Beach. His railway opened the east coast to settlers and winter visitors, and a trace of it can still be seen inland. The pier, first built in the 1920s, has been damaged by hurricanes more than once and rebuilt, and it is a favourite place for fishing and for watching the sun come up over the water.

For riders, A1A is a gentle pleasure, a road of easy curves, with sea views, palm trees and sand blowing over the tarmac in places. The surface is generally good, though storms have eaten away at the dunes and the road in places, and the shoulders can be narrow. Traffic is moderate, thicker on weekends. Wind off the ocean can be strong, and sudden thunderstorms in summer arrive with huge rain and lightning, so keep an eye on the sky. Nesting sea turtles use the beaches in summer, and some areas are lit with turtle-friendly lights.

To the north, Marineland, which opened in 1938 and claims to be the world's first oceanarium, is close, and to the south lies Washington Oaks Gardens, with its shore of coquina rock and formal gardens. Fuel and supermarkets are available in the town and in Palm Coast, about fifteen kilometres away. Early morning is magical, with the light on the water and pelicans skimming the waves, and a cup of coffee on the pier is a fine way to start the day.
t.zaraysk@54.8,38.9:
Zaraysk is a small town with a very long memory. Some twenty thousand years ago, Ice Age hunters camped on the banks of the Oka near here, and the archaeological site they left behind yielded carved mammoth-ivory figurines, including small female statuettes, some of the oldest works of art found in Russia. The town itself first appears in chronicles in the thirteenth century, linked to a famous icon of St Nicholas, which was reputedly brought here from Crimea, and the name Nikola Zarazsky became a regional byword.

The centerpiece is the Kremlin, built in the 1520s of white stone under Grand Prince Vasily III as a southern outpost against Tatar raids. It is one of the few stone kremlins in the Moscow region, and one of the smallest in Russia, and it stands on a hill above the river with cathedrals inside its walls. The Cathedral of St Nicholas is a handsome building with tall belfry, and the walls and corner towers are well preserved. Fyodor Dostoevsky spent boyhood summers on his father's small estate at Darovoye, a few kilometers from here, and his experiences of village life fed his novels, a connection the town takes pride in.

Riding is easy and rural. The road from Kolomna runs south across the Oka floodplain, with long, flat stretches, wide fields and views of river meanders, and the surface is generally decent on the main roads. Villages with wooden houses, painted shutters and wells appear at intervals, and storks and cranes nest on poles. Wind can be strong on the open plain, and summer thunderstorms are sudden, so keep an eye on the sky. Farm vehicles, horse carts and the odd cow can appear on side roads.

Zaraysk is large enough for fuel, shops and cafes, and it is the best place to stop before the long run back or onward. The best months are May to September, with warm days and long light, though midsummer heat can be intense. Spring and autumn bring mud on the side roads, and winter is cold and snowy, with frost that can last for months. Local cooks make the most of the river's fish, and regional pastila, a soft apple sweet, is a speciality of nearby Kolomna.
t.serpukhov@54.9,37.4:
Serpukhov is a town on the Oka that has been the southern guard post of Moscow for seven centuries. In the fourteenth century it was the seat of a small principality ruled by Prince Vladimir the Brave, a cousin and comrade of Dmitry Donskoy, who led the Serpukhov regiments at the great battle of Kulikovo in 1380. The town lay on the border between Moscow and its southern enemies, and a white-stone kremlin, built to keep the Tatars out, once stood above the river bend.

Today the old center is a quiet quarter of churches, merchant houses and a kremlin hill where the cathedral stands among surviving walls. Just outside, the Vysotsky Monastery, founded in 1374 by St Sergius of Radonezh, the most revered saint of medieval Russia, sits behind its walls near the Nara River, a peaceful, well-kept complex that holds the Icon of the Inexhaustible Cup, a revered image that draws pilgrims. The town later grew rich on textiles, and its brick mills and old merchants' mansions recall that era.

The riding in the district is a pleasure of its own. Roads south and west follow the Oka through bluffs, pine woods and meadow, and the river's high western bank has chalky cliffs and ravines. The Polenovo estate, home of the painter Vasily Polenov, lies on the river a short ride away, and the nearby town of Tarusa, a gentle riverside settlement, has long drawn writers and artists. The main road, the M2 from Moscow to Tula, is fast and busy, with heavy truck traffic, but the secondary roads are quieter, if patchy.

Serpukhov, with more than a hundred thousand residents, has all the services you need, with fuel at many stations, supermarkets and cafes. It is the right place to start or end a day on the Oka. The best seasons are late May to June, with fresh green and cool nights, and September, when the meadows go golden. High summer can be hot and the roads busy on weekends with city dwellers, and spring thaw brings potholes and mud, so check the surface before pushing the pace. Deer and wild boar are common in the woods at dusk.
t.solotcha@54.8,39.8:
South of Ryazan, where the Oka loops through meadows and pinewood, Solotcha is a quiet suburb that in practice feels like a village that has been left to itself. It sits on the left bank of the river, and the road in from the city runs for about twenty kilometres through forest and fields, so the transition from the city to this green and sandy country is quick. For a rider coming from Moscow, the landscape is a gentle introduction to the Meshchera lowlands, a flat, forested, lake-studded region of central Russia that writers like Konstantin Paustovsky made famous.

The star of the place is the Solotcha Monastery, a women's convent on the river bank with white walls and soft-coloured towers. It was founded in the late fourteenth century, in the time of the Ryazan princes, and was for centuries an important religious house of the Ryazan land. The monastery went through hard years in the Soviet era, when the buildings were used for other purposes, and has since been restored and reopened. Its grounds are quiet and mannered, the sort of place where you lower your voice without being told.

Not far away lies Konstantinovo, the birthplace of the poet Sergei Yesenin, whose verses about the Oka, birch trees and village life are part of Russian schooling. The museum there and the surrounding fields tie the two places together, which is why the ride from Ryazan out to the countryside has been a favourite excursion.

The roads here are mostly flat and smooth near the city, and then become patchier as you move into the villages. Expect long straight sections, some tar repairs and farm traffic, and do not expect dramatic corners. The pleasure is in the broad river valley, the pine smell on a warm day, and the way the light goes low and golden over the Oka in the evening. Summers are warm, and the sandy forest floor is full of mushrooms in autumn.

For fuel, Ryazan is twenty kilometres away and has everything, while Polyany, eight kilometres off, has a small town's services. In Solotcha itself, bring cash and patience, since it is a place for walking by the water, not for fuelling up or shopping.
t.tula@54.2,37.6:
Russians have a saying about carrying coals to Newcastle, and theirs is about taking your own samovar to Tula. The town has made samovars since the eighteenth century, and a museum of them stands in the center, with brass giants, tiny travelers' models and the elaborate urns used in merchant houses. Tula also made guns: Peter the Great founded an arms factory here in 1712, and the weapons works supplied the Russian army for centuries, so the old gunsmith's craft and the brass-tea tradition sit side by side. Add the gingerbread, spiced and printed with a pattern, and you have the three things Tula is known for.

The Kremlin is the visual center, a red-brick fortress finished in the early sixteenth century on the bank of the Upa River, with towers, thick walls and a cathedral inside. It is more compact and less ceremonial than Moscow's, and it served as a frontier stronghold against Crimean Tatar raids. Inside the walls, a pair of museums, one for weapons, the other for local history, are worth an hour. The city has a long, rather industrial skyline, but the old streets near the river retain a handsome, provincial charm.

Fourteen kilometers southwest lies Yasnaya Polyana, the estate where Leo Tolstoy was born in 1828, lived most of his life and wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina. The house is preserved with his study and library, the park has birch alleys and ponds, and his grave, a simple grassy mound in a patch of woods, is deliberately unmarked by a cross or inscription, as he wished. It is one of the most moving places in Russia, and well worth the ride.

Tula is a major city, so fuel, food and hotels are everywhere. The M2 highway links it to Moscow, about 180 kilometers north, and is fast but heavily used by trucks. The countryside to the south, near Kulikovo Field, where Dmitry Donskoy defeated the Mongol-Tatar forces in 1380, is open, rolling farmland with big skies. The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the roads are dry. Spring thaw and heavy winter snow make the side roads tricky, and summer heat can be intense on the open plain.
t.harbor springs@45.4,-85.0:
Harbor Springs is a small resort town on the north shore of Little Traverse Bay, in the top left corner of Michigan's mitten, and it has one of the nicest natural harbors on the Great Lakes. The bay is long and deep, sheltered from the big waves of Lake Michigan, and the town curves along its edge, with sailboats at anchor in the harbor and handsome summer houses on the hills. The area's Native name, Waganakising, meaning crooked tree, is still used by the Odawa people, whose community remains strong here.

The reason riders come is M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a narrow, twisting road that runs north along the bluffs above Lake Michigan toward Cross Village. For most of its length the road is roofed by branches, with beech, maple and birch crowding the pavement, and on a sunny afternoon the light flickers through the leaves like a film projector. The road is posted slow, with good reason: it is narrow, with tight bends, little shoulder and sudden breaks in the trees where the lake appears far below. In October the color is overwhelming, and the road is crowded, so go early.

Cross Village at the north end has an unusual landmark in Legs Inn, a restaurant built by a Polish immigrant out of driftwood and stone, with roots and chair legs forming its decorative facade, and a menu that leans on Polish dishes. South of Harbor Springs, Petoskey is a bigger town with a lively downtown. The beaches here yield Petoskey stones, pieces of fossil coral that are Michigan's state stone, which look like gray pebbles until they are wet. Ernest Hemingway spent boyhood summers on Walloon Lake nearby, and his early stories draw on northern Michigan.

Harbor Springs has fuel, a few places to eat and a handful of inns, but Petoskey, a short ride away, has the larger supermarkets and stations. The best times are June and September, when the weather is mild and the traffic light, and the first half of October for color. July and August are busy but beautiful. Winter brings heavy snow, and the Tunnel of Trees is not a winter road. Deer, often in groups, cross at dusk, so a slow pace is the sensible choice.
t.polenovo@54.7,37.2:
Polenovo is an estate on the high, wooded bank of the Oka River, and it is the Russian countryside of a painter's imagination. Vasily Polenov, a landscape artist of the late nineteenth century, bought the land in the 1890s and designed a house in a fanciful, medieval style, with a tower and wide terraces, where he lived and worked among fellow painters. The estate is now a museum-reserve, with the house, a church he designed and a gallery, and the surrounding landscape, a bend of the Oka with meadows and birch groves, looks very much as it did in his paintings.

The view from the terrace is the point. The Oka curves far below, wide and slow, with willows along its banks, and the far shore rolls away in soft blue distance, the kind of scene Russian painters tried to capture. In summer the meadows are full of wildflowers, in autumn the birches turn gold, and in winter the river freezes, with snow-covered banks. The nearby town of Tarusa, a gentle riverside settlement, became a refuge for writers and artists, and the poet Marina Tsvetaeva spent her childhood summers here.

The ride is relaxed. From Serpukhov or Tarusa, narrow country roads wind through villages, fields and pine woods, past wooden houses with carved window frames and wells. The surface varies, with good asphalt on main roads and patchy, sometimes broken pavement on the lanes, and the ferry or bridge crossings over the Oka can mean waits. Weekends in summer bring crowds of visitors to the museum, so early morning or a weekday is best, and rain turns unpaved lanes to mud quickly.

There are no big services at Polenovo itself, just a cafe near the entrance, so fill up in Tarusa, Serpukhov or Protvino. The best months are late May to September, with September particularly lovely, when the light is soft and the woods are turning. Winters are cold and snowy, and the estate is open year-round, but the roads are icy. Take your time, walk through the park, and watch the sun go down over the river.
t.st augustine@29.9,-81.3:
St Augustine has been going since 1565, when the Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed and founded a settlement, which makes it the oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the contiguous United States. That is more than half a century before the Pilgrims. The Spanish held it, lost it to the British, got it back, and finally ceded Florida to the United States in 1821, and the layers of all those flags show in the old street plan, narrow and tight, running between coquina-stone and stucco buildings.

The great landmark is the Castillo de San Marcos, a star-shaped fortress finished in the late seventeenth century and built from coquina, a soft limestone made of compressed shells. When English cannon balls hit it in a siege in 1702, they stuck in the stone rather than shattering it, which is exactly the story the guides like to tell. You can walk the walls and look across the Matanzas River toward the lighthouse on Anastasia Island. The town also owes a lot to Henry Flagler, the oil tycoon who built grand hotels here in the 1880s and a railway down the coast, and whose Ponce de Leon Hotel is now part of Flagler College. A well-known spring claims to be the Fountain of Youth, for the explorer Juan Ponce de León, who landed on this coast in 1513. The claim is more cheerful than historical.

For a rider the town is a place to arrive slowly. The Bridge of Lions brings Highway A1A over the Matanzas from the island, and the old centre is a grid of narrow streets full of tourists, horse-drawn carriages, trolleys, and one-way systems. The pavement is uneven in places, and parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, but still crowded at weekends. The coastal run of A1A north and south is flat, easygoing and often right on the dunes, with good views of the sea and a warm, salty smell in the air. Summer thunderstorms are frequent, and winter is mild and the best time to ride.

St Augustine has everything: petrol on the main roads, seafood restaurants, ice cream, coffee and plenty of places to sleep. Park near the old Plaza, walk the length of St George Street, and give yourself time for the fort. The town is crowded at midday and quieter in the evening, when the old buildings glow in the lamplight.
t.kozyrevsk@56.1,159.9:
Kozyrevsk is a village of about twelve hundred people on the Kamchatka River, set in the broad central valley of the peninsula between two long lines of volcanoes. The river here is wide and brown with glacier silt, flowing north through flat country of poplar, willow and larch, and in clear weather the cones along the horizon look almost unreal, white against a pale sky. This is the heart of one of the most active volcanic regions on the planet, and the ground and the weather both remind you of it.

The road from Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky to Klyuchi passes through here, and it is the main artery of the north of the peninsula. Expect a mix of good asphalt and long sections of gravel or patched surface, with grit and dust in summer and mud after rain. Bends are gentle and the land is flat, so the real challenge is distance and the weather, because fog, wind and sudden rain can arrive from either coast. July to September is the realistic window, with long light and warmer days. Ash from active volcanoes sometimes dusts the road and the air, so carry eye protection and a cloth for your face.

Fuel and food are limited. Kozyrevsk has a shop and a place or two to eat, and it can arrange a bed for the night, but the next proper supplies are at Klyuchi, some fifty kilometres ahead, and the capital is a very long way back. Fill the tank before you come, carry water, and do not count on the last pump being open. In summer, locals sell dried and smoked salmon from tables beside the road, and the fish is better than anything you will find in a supermarket.

The great draw is the line of volcanoes on the eastern horizon, including Kamen, Klyuchevskaya Sopka and Bezymianny. Klyuchevskaya, at around 4,750 metres, is the highest active volcano in Eurasia, and on a calm morning its plume of steam is visible from the village. The cones and the smell of sulphur and cold ash give the place a quiet drama, and the land seems newly formed. Wander down to the river at dusk, watch the light on the snow, and feel how small one rider is in a very big landscape.
t.as salt the place of tolerance and urban:
As-Salt climbs three steep hills in the Balqa highlands north-west of Amman, a town of honey-coloured limestone houses with arched windows, terraced streets and long staircases. In the late Ottoman period, from the 1860s to the 1920s, it was the most important town in the region east of the Jordan, a trading hub where merchants from Nablus, Damascus and Beirut settled and built grand houses in a mix of local and European styles. Muslims and Christians lived side by side, sharing guesthouses and charitable traditions, and the town was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2021 as As-Salt, the Place of Tolerance and Urban Hospitality.

When Amman was chosen as the capital of Transjordan in the 1920s, As-Salt lost its political role and slowly declined, which helped preserve its historic centre. Today it is a lively town of around eighty thousand, with a busy souk on Hammam Street, mosques and churches, and old mansions, some converted into museums and cultural centres, such as Abu Jaber House, now the Historic Old Salt Museum.

The landscape around As-Salt is hilly and fertile, with olive groves, vineyards and fields, and in spring, the hills are green and covered in wildflowers. West of the town, the road drops dramatically into the Jordan Valley, more than a thousand metres below, with hairpin bends and views toward the West Bank and, on clear days, Jerusalem. The descent to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on earth, is one of the great rides in the region, though the heat at the bottom can be fierce.

Riding in Jordan is generally straightforward, though driving can be aggressive in the cities, with fast traffic and unexpected manoeuvres. Fuel is easy to find in towns. As-Salt has narrow, steep streets, so leave the bike at the edge of the old town and walk. Try mansaf, the Jordanian national dish of lamb cooked in fermented yoghurt and served over rice, and kunafa, the sweet cheese pastry. Spring and autumn are ideal, when the hills are green or golden and the air is mild.
t.tel megiddo@32.6,35.2:
From the top of Tel Megiddo, the whole of the Jezreel Valley spreads out below you, a green and gold checkerboard of fields stretching towards Mount Tabor and the hills of Galilee. You can see at once why so many armies fought here. The mound guarded the narrow pass where the ancient coastal road, the Via Maris, crossed from the Mediterranean plain into the valley, and anyone who held it controlled one of the great trade and military routes of the ancient world.

The tel is made of more than twenty layers of cities, built one on top of the other over several thousand years. Excavations have revealed Canaanite temples, palaces, city gates and a remarkable water system, a shaft and tunnel cut through the rock to reach a spring outside the walls, which you can walk through today. The pharaoh Thutmose III recorded his victory at Megiddo in the fifteenth century before Christ, one of the first battles in history described in detail. The name gave rise to Armageddon, the site of the final battle in the Book of Revelation, and the place carries that weight. With Hazor and Beersheba, it is part of a UNESCO listing of biblical tels.

Megiddo lies in northern Israel near Kibbutz Megiddo and the road junction where Route 65 through Wadi Ara meets the valley; Umm el-Fahm is the nearest large town. The roads here are mostly fast and busy, with long straights across the valley floor and gentle climbs into the hills, and drivers can be assertive. Summer temperatures soar, so ride early and take water. Winter brings occasional heavy rain that makes surfaces slick.

Given the conflict in the region, check current travel advice carefully before planning a visit, and be prepared for checkpoints and changing security conditions. Fuel stations are common along the main roads, and the national park has a visitor centre with refreshments. Nearby towns serve excellent hummus, falafel and grilled meats, and in spring the valley fields are lush and green, shading to straw by early summer.
t.tyre@33.3,35.2:
Tyre was already ancient when Alexander the Great arrived in 332 before Christ. Then it was an island city just off the coast of what is now southern Lebanon, famously rich and famously stubborn, and when its citizens refused to open their gates, Alexander built a causeway out to the island and besieged it for months. Sand piled up against that causeway over the centuries, and the island became the peninsula you see today, with the modern city of Tyre spreading across it and the old harbour still busy with fishing boats.

The Phoenicians of Tyre were the great seafarers of the ancient Mediterranean, founding colonies as far away as Carthage, and they grew rich on purple dye extracted from murex sea snails, a colour so costly that it became the mark of emperors. The ruins listed by UNESCO are mostly Roman and Byzantine: colonnaded streets running down to the sea at the Al-Mina site, and at Al-Bass a vast necropolis, a monumental arch and one of the largest Roman hippodromes ever found, where chariot races once drew tens of thousands of spectators. The light here, reflected off the sea and the pale stone, has a particular soft brilliance.

Tyre is the main city of the south, with a lively souk, fish restaurants on the harbour and long sandy beaches south of town, part of which is a nature reserve where turtles nest. The coastal highway north towards Sidon and Beirut is busy, fast and chaotic, with drivers who take creative approaches to lanes, and side roads inland climb into hills of olive groves and tobacco fields. The southern border region has seen repeated conflict, including heavy fighting in recent years, so check current travel advice and the security situation carefully before going.

Fuel stations are frequent in and around the city, and food is excellent: grilled fish, fattoush, hummus and fresh bread, followed by sweet pastries and strong coffee. Spring and autumn bring the most comfortable riding weather, while summers are humid and hot. If you can, watch the sun set over the sea from the old harbour, where fishermen mend their nets much as they have done for millennia.
t.byblos@34.1,35.6:
Byblos, known to the Lebanese as Jbeil, is one of the contenders for the title of oldest continuously inhabited town on the planet. People have lived on this little headland above the Mediterranean for around seven thousand years, and the Phoenician city here was a great trading port, sending cedar wood from the mountains to Egypt and taking papyrus in return. The Greeks named the city after the papyrus, byblos, and from that word comes the word Bible. The alphabet developed by the Phoenicians, ancestor of Greek and Latin letters, is famously inscribed on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram, found here and now in Beirut's national museum.

The archaeological site lays out the whole sweep of history: Neolithic huts, Bronze Age temples including the Temple of the Obelisks, Roman columns and a small theatre, all overlooked by a Crusader castle built partly from older stone. Below it, the old souk and the little fishing harbour are a pleasant place to wander, with seafood restaurants and the sound of the sea against the old harbour walls.

The coastal highway from Beirut to Tripoli runs past the town, and riding it is an experience: fast, chaotic, crowded with cars, vans and scooters changing lanes with little warning. The real riding lies inland. Roads climb steeply from the coast into the Mount Lebanon range, up the Nahr Ibrahim valley, the river of Adonis, whose waters are said to run red in spring with the blood of the dying god, towards the Afqa grotto and the high villages. The mountain roads are narrow, with tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular views, and surfaces vary greatly. Spring and autumn are ideal; summer on the coast is hot and humid.

Jbeil has fuel, food and plenty of places to stay. Lebanese food is a joy: mezze of hummus, tabbouleh and fattoush, grilled fish and local wines from the Bekaa. Before riding in Lebanon, check current travel advice carefully, as the security situation can change quickly, and expect checkpoints on some roads. Respect local customs, and enjoy the warm welcome the country is known for.
t.mamshit@31.0,35.1:
Mamshit sits on a low spur above a dry riverbed in the northern Negev, a few kilometres east of Dimona, and from a distance it looks like nothing more than a heap of pale stones. Up close it becomes a town: streets, courtyards, staircases, arches, two Byzantine churches with mosaic floors and a set of large houses built by people who knew how to live comfortably in a hard place. This was Mampsis, a Nabataean settlement on the caravan routes that carried incense and spices from Arabia across the desert to the Mediterranean ports, and it shares a World Heritage inscription with Avdat, Haluza and Shivta as one of the desert cities of the Incense Route.

The Nabataeans, the same people who carved Petra, were masters of water. At Mamshit they built dams across the wadi below the town to catch the rare winter floods, storing the water in reservoirs for the dry months. Later the Romans and Byzantines took over, and the town reached its peak in the late Roman period; one house yielded a hoard of more than ten thousand silver coins. Today it is the smallest and perhaps the most complete of the Negev cities, and on a quiet morning you may have it almost to yourself.

The surrounding landscape is pure desert: bare hills of ochre and grey, deep wadis, the craters of the central Negev a little further south and, to the east, the long descent to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on earth. Route 25 heading east from Dimona drops through some spectacular twisting desert country towards the Arava valley, and the Ma'ale Akrabim, the Scorpion's Ascent, an old serpentine road nearby, is one of the most dramatic descents in Israel, though its state and access should be checked before you commit.

Dimona, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and simple food; Yeroham and Arad further on have more. Heat is the main hazard: from May to October middays are fierce, and the wind can whip up dust storms in hours. Carry plenty of water and ride early. The light at sunrise and sunset, when the stones of Mamshit glow honey and rose, is reason enough to time your visit carefully.
t.ancient jericho tell es sultan@31.9,35.4:
Jericho is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns on earth, and at Tell es-Sultan, on its northern edge, archaeologists have dug down through layers of settlement more than ten thousand years old. Among the finds is a great stone tower, built in the Neolithic, around eleven thousand years ago, long before writing, metal or the wheel, which is often called the oldest such tower in the world. The tell, with its trenches and mud brick walls, was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2023.

Jericho lies in the Jordan valley, some two hundred and fifty metres below sea level, and the low altitude gives it a warm climate even in winter, when people from Jerusalem come down for sunshine. Spring water from the Ein es-Sultan, the spring beside the tell, made it an oasis of palms, bananas and citrus in the desert. The Mount of Temptation rises to the west, with a Greek Orthodox monastery clinging to the cliff, reached by a cable car from near the tell. Hisham's Palace, an eighth century Umayyad palace with a superb mosaic of a lion and gazelles under a tree, is just north of town.

The road down from Jerusalem drops more than a kilometre in height through the Judean desert, a dramatic descent with bare hills and Bedouin camps. In summer the heat in the valley is extreme, often over forty degrees, and riding at midday is punishing. Winter and spring are the best seasons.

Jericho is in the Palestinian territories, in the West Bank, and travel here involves checkpoints and security issues that can change quickly; insurance for rental vehicles may not cover entry, so check carefully before planning a visit and follow your government's travel advice. The town has fuel, restaurants and markets selling dates, fruit and vegetables. Try the local dates and fresh juice, and the musakhan, chicken roasted with onions and sumac on flatbread.
t.birthplace of jesus church of the nativi:
To enter the Church of the Nativity, you have to bow. The main door into the basilica was made smaller over the centuries, probably to stop people riding in on horseback, and the low opening is known as the Door of Humility. Inside, the church built by Justinian in the sixth century over an earlier fourth century basilica of Constantine is one of the oldest functioning churches in the world, and beneath its altar a stair leads down to the Grotto of the Nativity, where a silver star marks the place where tradition says Jesus was born. The church and the pilgrimage route through Bethlehem became a World Heritage Site in 2012.

The church is shared by Greek Orthodox, Armenian and Catholic communities under an old arrangement called the Status Quo, which governs who cleans, lights and repairs what. A major restoration in recent years revealed mosaics and wooden beams hidden under grime, and the interior is brighter than it has been for centuries. Queues for the grotto can be long, especially at Christmas and Easter.

Bethlehem sits on a ridge south of Jerusalem, in the hills of Judea, with terraced olive groves and the Judean desert falling away to the east. Manger Square, in front of the church, is the heart of town, with shops selling olive wood carvings and mother of pearl, crafts that local families have practised for generations. The separation barrier between Bethlehem and Jerusalem, covered with graffiti and murals, is a stark presence on the northern edge of town.

Bethlehem is in the West Bank, and access involves checkpoints and security considerations that can change, so check the current situation and your government's advice before travelling. The streets are steep, narrow and crowded, and parking is difficult, so leave the bike outside the centre and walk. Fuel and food are easy to find. Try the falafel, hummus and knafeh, a sweet cheese pastry soaked in syrup.
t.sites of human evolution at mount carmel:
In the caves of Nahal Me'arot, on the western slope of Mount Carmel near the coast south of Haifa, people lived on and off for half a million years, and both Neanderthals and early modern humans left their bones here. The four caves, Tabun, Jamal, el-Wad and Skhul, contain one of the longest records of human evolution anywhere, and they were listed as a World Heritage Site in 2012. Tabun alone has layers spanning hundreds of thousands of years. The Natufian culture, among the first people to settle in villages before farming, also left traces in el-Wad.

The caves are set in a limestone cliff above the coastal plain, with views west over fields and fishponds toward the sea. A nature reserve protects the site, and paths lead to the cave entrances, with displays explaining the finds. The Carmel's slopes are covered with Mediterranean scrub, oak and pine, and in spring wildflowers bloom everywhere.

The coastal road south from Haifa passes the site, and the Crusader fortress at Atlit, on the coast nearby, is still a military zone. Inland, the Carmel ridge rises to over five hundred metres, with Druze villages such as Daliyat al-Karmel and Isfiya on the summit; the Druze markets sell spices, sweets and crafts, and the restaurants serve excellent food. The Muhraka, a Carmelite monastery on the spot where tradition places the contest between Elijah and the prophets of Baal, has wide views over the Jezreel valley.

The roads over the Carmel ridge are twisting and scenic, climbing through forest with views over the sea and the valleys. A big fire in 2010 burned large areas of forest, which is slowly recovering. Traffic can be heavy near Haifa. Summer is hot and humid on the coast.

Daliyat al-Karmel, eight kilometres away, is the nearest reliable place for fuel and a meal, and Haifa has everything. Check current security conditions and travel advice before visiting the region.
t.ancient city of damascus@33.5,36.3:
Damascus claims, with plenty of justification, to be among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Its old city, enclosed by Roman and medieval walls, holds the Umayyad Mosque, built in the early eighth century on the site of a Roman temple and a Christian church, with golden mosaics showing an idealised landscape of rivers and palaces, and a shrine said to hold the head of John the Baptist. The Street Called Straight, mentioned in the story of Saint Paul's conversion, still runs east to west through the old city, and the covered Souk al-Hamidiyya, with its iron roof pierced by bullet holes from the 1920s, leads to the mosque.

The old city is a maze of lanes, courtyard houses, khans, hammams and churches, where Muslims and Christians have lived side by side for centuries. The Azem Palace, an eighteenth century Ottoman residence, and the tomb of Saladin, beside the Umayyad Mosque, are among the highlights. The city was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1979, and placed on the list in danger during the civil war.

The city lies at the foot of Mount Qasioun, at the edge of the desert, where the Barada river once made a green oasis, the Ghouta, of orchards and gardens. The war devastated much of the surrounding area, and the scars are visible.

Syria's situation has changed dramatically since late 2024, and it remains unstable. Most governments advise against all travel, and practical matters such as insurance, fuel supply, money and border crossings are uncertain. Riding here is not something to undertake without very careful research and up to date local knowledge. If and when travel becomes safer, the old city, its food, from shawarma to sweets like baklava and booza ice cream, and its people will be the reward.

Fuel and services exist in the city, but supply can be unreliable. Traffic is chaotic, and the old city is best explored on foot.
t.area 1@31.7,35.1:
The hills south of Jerusalem and Bethlehem are older than most of the countries now claiming them, and the terraced slopes around Battir are among the best evidence. For centuries, perhaps for two thousand years, farmers here have built dry-stone terraces down the steep valley sides to grow olives, grapes, figs and vegetables, and the water that feeds them comes from springs and is shared out through channels according to a rota among local families. The system was recognised as a World Heritage landscape in 2014, under the title of the land of olives and vines in southern Jerusalem.

The village of Battir is known for its small, flavourful aubergines, which locals call the Battiri variety, and for the old railway line that runs through the bottom of the valley. That line was built by the Ottomans in the 1890s to link Jaffa with Jerusalem, and after 1948 it became part of the armistice line, which is part of why the valley stayed undeveloped. Today you can walk along the valley floor and look up at terraces that have not changed much in many generations.

It is worth being plain about the riding. The roads in this area are narrow, steep and twisting, with tight bends and blind crests, patchy tarmac and a lot of local traffic, and the region is politically sensitive, with checkpoints, barriers and changing access conditions that no map keeps up with. Check the current situation locally before you set out, ride with respect and in daylight, and keep your documents with you. In spring the slopes are green and wildflowers are everywhere; in summer the hills are bleached and hot, and in autumn the olive harvest brings families out onto the terraces.

For fuel and food, Husan, a couple of kilometres away, and the nearby town of Bethlehem are the practical choices, and there are small cafes in the villages where a coffee and something sweet will not cost much. Bring water, because the terraces offer little shade, and wear shoes you can walk in, since the best part of this place is on foot.
t.mansion of mazra ih@33.0,35.1:
The Baháʼí faith has two of its holiest places in Israel, and the Mansion of Mazra'ih is the quieter of them. It stands in the farmland north of Acre, near the coast, a large Ottoman-era house surrounded by gardens and orange trees. Bahá'u'lláh, the founder of the religion, spent years as a prisoner in the fortress city of Acre, and when his confinement was relaxed in 1877 he moved here, living in the mansion for a couple of years before settling at nearby Bahjí, where he died in 1892.

The mansion and its gardens are part of the Baháʼí Holy Places in Haifa and the Western Galilee, which UNESCO listed in 2008. Visitors are welcome in the gardens, and the atmosphere is calm and formal, with clipped hedges, paths and a pervasive scent of citrus and jasmine. Dress modestly, expect to follow instructions from the staff, and be ready for questions about photographs. The mansion has an interesting history before it became a holy place, having been a country house of an Ottoman governor.

Acre itself, a few kilometres south, is an extraordinary old port city with crusader halls and Ottoman walls, listed by UNESCO in 2001, and it is a short and easy ride. The coastal road, Route 4, runs north to Nahariya and past some good beaches, and inland the hills of the Western Galilee are cut by roads with tight bends and views over olive groves and small Arab and Druze villages. Traffic can be heavy, driving habits are brisk, and the hot, humid summer afternoons are best spent in the shade; spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.

Nahariya, about two kilometres away, has fuel, a seafront promenade and plenty of cafes, and Acre has famous hummus places in the old city, which you eat sitting at a plain table with a big pile of pickles. Opening times for religious sites vary with holidays and the Sabbath, so check before you go, and be aware that the security situation in the north can change quickly.
t.tel hazor@33.0,35.6:
If you stand on the top of Tel Hazor on a clear day, the view is of the Hula valley to the north and the hills of Upper Galilee to the west, with the snow-capped hump of Mount Hermon, in winter, sitting at the far end. The tel itself is a vast, flat-topped mound, the largest ancient site in Israel's north, rising out of the fields near Kibbutz Ayelet HaShahar. It is what archaeologists call a tel, a hill made of the layers of cities built one on top of another over thousands of years.

Hazor was one of the great Canaanite cities of the Bronze Age, with a large lower city as well as the high mound, and it appears in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts and in the Bible, where it is described as destroyed by Joshua. Excavations have found a palace, temples, a huge water system and cuneiform tablets, and later layers show the city fortified under Israelite kings, before the Assyrians destroyed it in 732 BC. It was listed by UNESCO in 2005 along with Megiddo and Beersheba.

The ride here is on good main roads. Route 90 runs the length of the Jordan rift, through the Hula valley, where in winter thousands of cranes and other migrating birds gather in the wetlands, and the climb to Safed on Route 89 is a good road with a series of bends and views down to the Sea of Galilee. The Golan Heights to the east are a long climb with open views, and in spring the fields are carpeted with wildflowers. Summer is hot and dry in the valley and cooler on the hills, and winter can be wet and cold.

For fuel, Rosh Pinna, a few kilometres away, has stations and cafes, and the city of Safed above it is a place of old synagogues, artists' quarters and winding lanes, where cheese and hot drinks are easy to find. The site itself has shade only in small amounts, so take a hat and water, and allow time to walk the mound.
t.quseir amra@31.8,36.6:
Qusayr Amra stands alone in the stony desert of eastern Jordan, in the Wadi Butm, about twenty-five kilometres from Azraq and some eighty from Amman. It is a small, low building of pale stone with three barrel-vaulted halls and a bathhouse, built in the early eighth century under the Umayyad caliphs, and its plain exterior hides some of the most surprising paintings in the early Islamic world.

The interior walls and ceilings are covered with frescoes. They show hunting scenes, musicians and dancers, bathing women, and figures of kings, and in the small domed bath chamber the sky is painted as a map of the constellations. Pictures of people, and especially of nude women, were later forbidden or avoided in much of the Muslim world, which makes these paintings unusually revealing about the life of the court. The building was probably a retreat and bathhouse for a prince, perhaps the future caliph al-Walid II, who loved hunting, wine and poetry. UNESCO listed it in 1985, and it has been restored with international help.

The way there is part of the desert castles circuit, a loop of Umayyad and Roman remains east of Amman. The main road, Highway 40, heads east from the capital towards Azraq, mostly straight and fast across a stony plateau of black basalt and pale flint, and it carries a steady stream of trucks heading for Saudi Arabia and Iraq, so overtaking calls for patience. There are no corners to speak of, but the wind is often strong and sudden, and the heat in summer is severe, with the ground reflecting like an oven. Spring and autumn are better, and the light in the late afternoon turns the desert gold. Winters can be bitterly cold and wet, and flash floods run down the wadis after heavy rain, so check the weather.

Fuel is a real consideration. There is little between Amman and Azraq, so fill the tank in Zarqa or in Azraq, a town of fifteen thousand people with a mix of Circassian and Druze communities. Azraq also has a wetland reserve, once a great oasis that has been mostly drained for the capital's water supply. Carry plenty of water and a hat,, and give your eyes a minute to adjust when you step into the dim rooms.
t.biblical tels megiddo@32.6,35.2:
Megiddo is the hill that gave the world the word Armageddon, which comes from Har Megiddo, the mount of Megiddo, and it sits where the Jezreel valley opens to the coast road, a little north of the Wadi Ara pass. The tell is a long mound made of some twenty layers of ruined cities piled on top of each other, and from its top the whole green plain stretches north to the hills of Nazareth. Today it is inscribed on the World Heritage list together with two other biblical mounds.

The reason for so many cities is geography. Whoever held Megiddo controlled the narrow pass through the Carmel ridge on the Via Maris, the road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, and so armies met here again and again. Pharaoh Thutmose III won a famous battle on the plain around 1457 BC, recorded in the temple at Karnak, and in 609 BC King Josiah of Judah was killed here when he tried to stop Pharaoh Necho marching north. The excavations reveal gates, a palace, stables or storehouses from the time of the Israelite kings, and a tunnel dug to reach a spring from inside the city walls, which you can walk through today. There is a good visitor centre, and the site gets very hot, so bring water and a hat.

The riding here is made up of fast roads and small, farm-lined lanes. Highway 66 and Highway 65 carry heavy traffic, with trucks, buses and impatient drivers, so concentrate and ride defensively, and rely on the smaller roads across the valley for more relaxed motoring through fields of cotton, sunflowers and wheat, with fish ponds and kibbutz farms. The road through Wadi Ara towards Umm al-Fahm climbs gently through hills, with views to the sea from higher points. Spring is the best time, when the fields are green and the flowers are out; summer is hot and hazy, and the air feels heavy in the valley.

Fuel is easy to find on the main roads, with stations at the junctions and in the larger towns such as Afula, Umm al-Fahm and Haifa, but you should check local conditions and any security advice before choosing routes, since the situation in the region can change quickly. Cafes and simple restaurants are on the main roads, and hummus, fresh bread and strong coffee are always on offer.
t.house of abbud@32.9,35.1:
Acre sits at the northern tip of Haifa Bay, on a small peninsula that has been a port since the Bronze Age, and the House of Abbud is one of the Ottoman-era buildings of its old town, in a maze of stone lanes about a kilometre from the walls.

Two layers of history are stacked here. The Crusaders held Acre from 1104 and made it their main port after losing Jerusalem, and the halls of the Knights Hospitaller, vast vaulted spaces half buried under later buildings, are among the most atmospheric rooms in the country. Visitors can also walk through a tunnel dug by the Templars. The city fell to the Mamluks in 1291, ending the Crusader presence on the mainland. Centuries later, in the late eighteenth century, the Ottoman governor Ahmad al-Jazzar rebuilt it, with the great mosque that bears his name, the caravanserai called Khan al-Umdan and the massive sea walls that stopped Napoleon in 1799. Today the old city is a living, mostly Arab neighbourhood with fishermen, markets, and children playing among the stones.

Not far to the north, at Bahji, the Baha'i Faith has its holiest shrine and a garden, which UNESCO inscribed together with the shrines of Haifa in 2008. The coast road, Route 4, runs from Haifa through Acre to Nahariya and the border at Rosh Hanikra, with white cliffs and sea caves, and the fast roads are busy with traffic. Inland, the hills of the western Galilee have good riding with bends, olive groves and villages, though you should check local conditions before choosing routes, since the situation in the region can change.

The old town is meant to be walked. Park outside the walls, near the harbour or at the car park by the land gate, because the lanes are narrow and some are steps. Acre has a hot, humid summer, with the best weather in spring and October. The fish restaurants on the harbour, the hummus places in the souk and the sweet shops with kunafa are the real draw. Fuel is on the main roads around Acre and in the nearby towns of Kiryat Yam and Nahariya.
t.incense route desert cities in the negev:
The Negev is not the empty wasteland it appears to be from a plane. From roughly the third century BC to the second century AD, the Nabataeans, a people of Arabian origin who made their capital at Petra, ran one of the most profitable trades in the ancient world through it, carrying frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean ports of Gaza. They controlled the water, building cisterns, dams and terraced fields to farm in an area with almost no rain, and along the route they raised caravan stations, forts and small cities, among them Avdat, Haluza, Mamshit and Shivta, which UNESCO listed together in 2005 as the Incense Route Desert Cities.

Spring brings a thin green, and after rain, flash floods can thunder down the wadis with no warning, so keep out of dry channels if clouds are around. Summer midday temperatures are brutal, and winter nights can be cold, so the best months for riding are March, April, October and November.

The riding is among the most atmospheric in the Middle East. Long, wide roads cross empty plateaus and drop in switchbacks into the deep valleys, with views over the crater of Makhtesh Ramon, the largest erosion crater in the world, near Mitzpe Ramon. Expect strong crosswinds on exposed stretches, and watch for camels and ibex wandering onto the road at dusk. Gravel on the shoulders can be treacherous.

Fuel is the practical question. The desert has long gaps between towns, and Mitzpe Ramon, a small town of a few thousand people on the crater's rim, is the reliable stop, so top up there, and carry water. Check the current security situation and military zones before heading off the main roads, since parts of the Negev contain firing ranges and border areas.

Stand still for a few minutes in the evening when the sun drops and the chalk goes pink, and the silence of the desert will tell you more about the old trade than any sign.
t.crac des chevaliers and qal at salah el:
Crac des Chevaliers stands on a spur of the Jebel Ansariyya, overlooking the Homs Gap, the one low corridor between the Mediterranean coast and the Syrian interior, and that is why it was built here. In 1142 the Count of Tripoli gave the site to the Knights Hospitaller, who rebuilt it over the following century into the greatest castle of the Crusades, with two concentric rings of walls, a moat, a long, sloping ramp, and a great hall with Gothic vaults. At its peak it could hold a garrison of some two thousand men, with stables, storerooms and an enormous cistern.

Saladin passed it by in 1188, deciding that it was too strong to take. The Mamluk sultan Baibars finally forced its surrender in 1271, reportedly with a forged letter instructing the knights to surrender. After that it served the Mamluks and later the Ottomans, and eventually villagers set up homes inside the walls. T. E. Lawrence, who walked here as a young Oxford student in 1909, called it perhaps the best-preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world. UNESCO listed it in 2006, along with Qal'at Salah El-Din, another castle in Syria's coastal mountains.

The fighting of the Syrian civil war reached the castle in 2012 and caused damage to its upper works, and the country has been difficult and unsafe for visitors for many years. Anyone thinking of riding here needs to look at current travel advice and the realities of borders and permits before going anywhere near it, and the ride titles listing Baalbek in Lebanon are best treated as armchair material for now.

What a rider notices on the ground is the landscape. The Homs Gap is a fertile corridor of olive groves, orchards and wheat between the Lebanon range and the Ansariyya hills. Wind funnels through it, and spring is very green, with rain until April. Roads in the area climb in bends to the castle, with a final approach that is steep and narrow. Tallkalakh and the surrounding towns would have fuel and food in normal times.

Even from a photograph, the scale of the place is hard to forget.
t.area 2@31.7,35.2:
Battir is a village of terraces. On the slopes of the hills south-west of Jerusalem, a system of stone-walled terraces and irrigation channels has been watered for centuries by a spring that is shared out in turn among the village families, according to a rota that locals still keep. The terraces grow vegetables, olives, and aubergines for which Battir is known, and the system, with its Roman-era origins and later improvements, was listed by UNESCO in 2014 as a cultural landscape. The little railway line from Jaffa to Jerusalem, built by the Ottomans in the 1890s, runs along the valley floor below the village.

South of here lie the area around Husan and Beit Jala and further toward Hebron, a landscape of limestone hills, terraced slopes, olive groves and old stone villages. The soil is stony and the light, particularly in spring and in the afternoon, is clear and golden. The Caves of Maresha and Bet Guvrin, on the ride titles, are a short ride to the west, a labyrinth of bell-shaped caves cut in soft chalk by Hellenistic and Roman quarrymen, and a very different kind of underground.

Riding here requires care and local knowledge. The area lies within the West Bank, with military checkpoints, restricted roads, and a complicated map of zones, and what is open to a foreign visitor on a motorbike can change with little notice. Check the current situation with reliable sources and ask locally before going, and be ready to turn back. The roads are narrow and winding in the hills, with sharp bends and steep drops, and traffic can be heavy, with sudden stops at junctions.

Water, a map and a flexible plan are worth more than a tight schedule.

When it works, the reward is quiet: the sound of water in a channel, the smell of wild thyme on the terraces, and the old railway line curving below.
t.tower@31.5,35.9:
Umm ar-Rasas rises out of the plateau east of the King's Highway with little warning, a walled rectangle of Byzantine and early Islamic ruins on a flat expanse of wheat fields and sheep. In ancient times it was called Kastron Mefaa, a Roman military camp that later developed into a town, and it remained inhabited through the Byzantine period and into the early Islamic centuries before it faded away. UNESCO listed it in 2004, and the most remarkable piece of the site is the floor of the Church of Saint Stephen, a mosaic from the eighth century that shows cities of the region in tiny, detailed vignettes, including Jerusalem and Philadelphia, the ancient name of Amman.

A kilometre or so to the north stands the tower. It is a single square pillar of dressed stone, about fourteen metres high, with a small room at the top, and it is one of very few surviving stylite towers, built for a hermit who lived on top in imitation of Simeon Stylites, the Syrian saint who spent decades on a pillar. The holy man seems to have lived alone on a platform exposed to the wind and sun, with food hauled up in a basket. It stands in a stubble field, with nothing around it but the horizon.

The ride to it is a good one. The King's Highway runs along the plateau edge between Madaba and Karak, crossing the deep gorge of Wadi Mujib on bends that drop and climb through dramatic scenery. The roads around Umm ar-Rasas are quiet and open, with desert wind, and the surface generally good, though shoulders can be sandy and sheep sometimes cross the tarmac. Spring is wonderful, with green fields and red poppies, and summer is hot and dry.

Fuel and food are in the larger towns. Madaba, famous for its Byzantine map mosaic, and Dhiban on the King's Highway are the sensible bets, and it is wise to start with a full tank. Bring water and a hat, because there is little shade at the site.

The silence in the stubble field is the best thing about the tower, and it is worth a few minutes of your day.
t.house of abdu llah pasha@32.9,35.1:
Acre, or Akko, is a walled port on the northern arm of Haifa Bay, and almost every century has left a layer on it. The Crusaders made it their last great stronghold in the Holy Land until it fell in 1291, and the vaulted halls of the Knights Hospitaller still lie underneath the Ottoman town built on top. The Ottomans rebuilt the walls in the eighteenth century, added the mosque of al-Jazzar, a caravanserai with a courtyard of columns, and a labyrinth of covered markets. The whole old city is a UNESCO site.

The House of 'Abdu'lláh Páshá belongs to a later and quieter chapter. It was a large Ottoman house in the old city, and it served as the residence of Bahá'u'lláh, the founder of the Bahá'í Faith, and his family after their years of confinement in the city's citadel in the 1860s and 1870s. It is among the Bahá'í holy places in Acre and the Galilee that UNESCO listed in 2008, together with the Shrine of Bahá'u'lláh at Bahjí north of the town and the gardens of Haifa. Visits to these places are arranged by the Bahá'í community and are not always possible, so check the arrangements rather than turning up and hoping.

For a rider, the old city is a place to walk. Cars and bikes are restricted in many lanes, and the streets are narrow, stepped and full of pedestrians and shopkeepers. Park outside the walls, near the harbour or the promenade, and go in on foot. The coast road, Route 4, runs north to Rosh HaNikra, where white chalk cliffs meet the sea, and south to Haifa, a busy but easy ride with the Carmel ridge on the skyline. East of Acre, the roads climb quickly into the hills of Galilee, with olive groves, stone villages and lively bends.

Acre has about forty-five thousand people, so fuel, shops and cafés are never a problem. Its food has a loyal following: hummus in small places near the market, fresh fish at the harbour, and sweets laced with rosewater and pistachio. The sea breeze keeps the heat tolerable in summer, but midday can still be sticky, and it is worth knowing that Friday afternoons and Saturdays are quiet, with many shops closed.

Walk the ramparts at sunset, when the old stone turns honey-coloured and the fishermen mend their nets below.
t.prison@32.9,35.1:
Acre's citadel has been a prison for much of its life, and the word on the label points to it. The great vaulted fortress in the north-west corner of the old city was built by the Ottomans on the foundations of the Hospitaller halls, and in the nineteenth century it became a feared jail for political prisoners. Bahá'u'lláh was held here in the late 1860s with his family and followers, in crowded and miserable conditions, before being moved to a house in the town. Later, under the British Mandate, the same building held Jewish underground fighters, and a dramatic break-out in 1947 became one of the best-known episodes of that period. Part of the complex is now a museum, and the rooms are open to the public on set hours.

It is a place of thick limestone walls, low arched ceilings, echoing stairs and windows that look onto the sea. The Mediterranean slaps at the base of the walls, and the air carries salt, diesel and frying onions from nearby kitchens. The fortress is also where Napoleon's army broke its teeth in 1799, when a long siege failed, a turning point that is commemorated in the town.

Approaching Acre by motorbike is simple until you reach the walls. The coast road is fast and well surfaced, and traffic is heavy at rush hour, with buses and delivery vans. The area near the harbour has parking for bikes, and the promenade along the sea wall is a pleasant place to stroll.

Practicalities are straightforward. There are fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets on the edge of town and small restaurants inside the walls, with Acre's population of over forty-five thousand to support them. El Mazra'a, a smaller place a few kilometres north, has fewer services.

Allow a couple of hours to walk the ramparts and the covered markets. In summer, the stone is hot by midday, so an early start and a hat are wise. Spring and autumn are gentler, and winter brings sharp storms that crash against the sea wall.
t.madaba@31.7,35.8:
Madaba is the town of mosaics, and the reason is a floor. In the Church of St George, a nineteenth-century Greek Orthodox building, lies a sixth-century Byzantine mosaic map of the Holy Land, made from some two million tiny stones, which shows Jerusalem, the Nile delta and the Dead Sea with astonishing detail. It came to light again in 1884 when the church was being built, and it remains the oldest known cartographic depiction of the region. Other churches and houses in town contain fine mosaics too, and a small archaeological park displays some of the best, so you can easily spend a morning looking at the floors.

The town sits on a plateau at roughly 780 metres, on the ancient Kings Highway, which in the Bible is the road the Israelites asked permission to use on their way to the Promised Land. It was an old trade route between Egypt and Syria, and Madaba had a significant Christian population from early times, which still makes up a notable minority in the town. A few kilometres to the northwest rises Mount Nebo, where Moses is said to have looked out over the land he would not enter, with a view across the Jordan valley to the Dead Sea on a clear day.

Riding in Jordan is easy and varied, but different from Europe. In Madaba the streets are busy, with minibuses, taxis and pedestrians weaving through, and speed bumps appear without warning. Once you leave town on the Kings Highway, the road runs south across a high, open plateau of wheat fields and olive groves, with sudden, dramatic plunges into the canyons, such as the Wadi Mujib, where the road drops hundreds of metres in long switchbacks. Police checkpoints are common and polite, and a passport and bike papers should be on hand. Summer afternoons can be fiercely hot, and spring brings wildflowers and cooler air.

Madaba is a town of about eighty thousand, with fuel stations, bakeries and many places to eat. Order a plate of hummus, grilled meat and fresh bread, and finish with sweet tea or Arabic coffee. The old town's small family-run restaurants are friendly. It is a good place to stock up on water and snacks before the long run south along the Kings Highway, because services between the larger towns can be sparse.
t.karak@31.2,35.7:
Karak is dominated by its castle, which sits on a spur above the town and looks as stern now as it did eight centuries ago. The Crusaders built it in the 1140s, under the kings of Jerusalem, to control the road between Damascus and Egypt and the pilgrim route to Mecca, and for a few decades it was one of the most important strongholds of the Latin East. Its most notorious lord, Reynald of Châtillon, raided Muslim caravans from here, and the dark vaulted corridors and cellars are a good place to imagine the sieges. In 1188, after a long blockade that followed the Battle of Hattin, Saladin took the castle, and it later passed to the Mamluks, who added their own towers and halls.

The town around it is a lively market place of about twenty thousand people, with the old stone buildings and narrow lanes of the old centre spreading across the hill. It is also the home of Jordan's national dish, mansaf, a feast of lamb cooked in a sauce of dried fermented yoghurt, served on a bed of rice and flatbread, and eaten with the right hand at weddings and celebrations. Karak is considered one of its heartlands, and a plate is a fine reward after the ride.

The road here is the Kings Highway, an ancient track that runs along the spine of the Transjordanian plateau. It is more scenic than the desert highway nearby, as it crosses deep wadis and climbs high ridges, with sweeping views toward the Dead Sea far below. The riding is a mix of smooth tarmac and patched sections, with plenty of tight bends, steep descents and the occasional goat or sheep on the road. Vehicles may overtake in unexpected places, so keep your guard up, and watch for sand and gravel on the surface. In winter the plateau can be cold and wet, and occasionally snowy, while summer heat is intense in the valleys.

Karak is a large enough town to have fuel stations, banks, shops and simple cafes. The castle is open daily, and a couple of hours is enough to explore it. Evening is a lovely time to be on the ramparts, when the stone turns gold and the call to prayer rises from the town below. From here, the road south leads past Dana and the crusader castle at Shobak to Petra, a long and spectacular day.
t.wawa@48.0,-84.8:
Wawa is famous for a goose. A huge steel statue of a Canada goose stands at the junction on the highway, put up in the 1960s, and the name itself comes from the Ojibwe word for the wild goose, which migrates over the lake in flocks each spring and autumn. The town, home to around twenty-six hundred people, grew up as a gold rush camp in the nineteenth century and later lived off the iron ore mines to the north, which have since closed.

It sits on Highway 17, the Trans-Canada, close to the northeastern shore of Lake Superior, where the road runs through low hills and spruce forest and sometimes glimpses the lake in a long grey-blue sweep.
