Superior is the biggest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, and its water is cold enough that it stays chilly to the touch even in August. The ride north from the Sault is long and mostly empty. The road is well surfaced but exposed, with long straights, rolling hills, frost heaves and occasional roadworks, and the wind off the lake can be strong and cold.

Wawa is a good place to stop because the services are real. There is fuel, there are motels, and there are diners where a plate of eggs and bacon or a fish dinner will set you up for the road. Michipicoten Bay and the river mouth are close by, and the Lake Superior Provincial Park, just to the south, is full of rock, beach and rivers that rest on the old Canadian Shield, among the oldest rock on earth.

Moose and bears are as common as cars at dusk, so be cautious. Summer from June to September is the riding season, and the shoulder months can bring snow. Bring a warm layer even on a sunny day, because the lake has its own weather.
t.debark@13.2,37.9:
Debark is a highland market town of about twenty-odd thousand people, high on the northern Ethiopian plateau at roughly the height of a Swiss mountain village, and it exists, in practical terms, because of the mountains behind it. The Simien range rises just north, and Debark is where the national park has its headquarters, where visitors check in, pay their fees and, if they plan to walk, pick up the armed scout the park requires. Riders arriving by road will mostly be coming from Gondar, about a hundred kilometres to the south-west, along a tarmac highway that climbs steadily through terraced farmland, eucalyptus groves and villages where the road doubles as the main street.

The riding in is a lesson in Ethiopian traffic. Goats, donkeys, cattle and children share the carriageway with minibuses and trucks, and nothing, ever, is in a hurry. Surfaces are generally decent on the main route but can break up without warning, and rain turns the shoulders to slick mud. It is a place for steady speeds and a lot of horn. Mornings are cold at nearly three thousand metres, so pack a warm layer, and the dry season from roughly October to March gives the clearest skies and the safest going.

The town itself is plain and busy, with a main road lined by cafés, small hotels and shops, and a market that draws farmers from the surrounding hills. Coffee is the thing to look for, served in small cups with a lot of ceremony, and injera with spicy stews if you want a proper meal. Fuel is generally available in a town this size, but supplies can run short in Ethiopia, so fill up whenever you see a working pump and carry what you can. Gondar, with its seventeenth-century castles built by emperor Fasilides and his successors, is the larger service point behind you.

What makes Debark matter is what it opens. The Simien Mountains were among the first places on Earth to be given UNESCO World Heritage status, in 1978, for their enormous escarpments, deep gorges and rare wildlife, including the walia ibex, found nowhere else, and the gelada baboon. Ras Dashen, Ethiopia's highest peak at around 4,550 metres, stands in the park. Debark is the last place to sort out supplies, cash and permissions before you go up.
t.simien mountains viewpoints@13.2,38.1:
East of Debark the land does something that plateau country is not supposed to do: it stops. The Simien escarpment drops away in vertical cliffs of well over a kilometre, a wall of basalt carved by millions of years of erosion into pinnacles, buttresses and gullies, and the view across it is among the great ones in Africa. The viewpoints strung along the park track, with names like Sankaber, Geech and Imet Gogo, each give a slightly different angle on the same astonishing void.

Getting there is a gravel ride rather than a tarmac one. The park road from Debark is unpaved, rocky in places and rutted after rain, and at heights of three thousand metres and above, a loaded bike works hard. Pace yourself and keep an eye on the weather. Afternoons can bring cloud and sudden cold, and the dry months from late autumn to early spring give the clearest views. Rules apply: you pay park fees at the gate, and guides or scouts are normally expected when you leave the vehicle track.

The wildlife is the other half of the reason to come. Gelada baboons, sometimes called bleeding-heart monkeys for the red patch on the chest, graze in huge troops along the cliff edges, shuffling across the grass on their haunches and ignoring human visitors with a grandeur that most aristocrats could not match. They are the last grass-eating primates in the world. With luck you will also see the walia ibex, with its heavy curved horns, perched on the ledges, and lammergeier vultures riding the updraughts at eye level.

The air is thin and clean, the grass pale gold, and giant lobelias poke up in the high ground like strange candelabras. Local farmers still work the lower slopes, so you will pass shepherds and children offering to sell you handmade trinkets. At night the temperature can drop close to freezing, and the stars are staggering. Bring layers, and if you can, stay a night.
t.tomoka state park@29.3,-81.1:
Tomoka State Park sits where the Tomoka and Halifax rivers meet on the Florida coast just north of Daytona, and it is a surprise after the busy beach towns: a quiet, shaded patch of old Florida where live oaks arch over the road, hung with Spanish moss, and the tidal creeks run slow and tea-coloured through salt marsh. The air smells of brackish water and warm pine needles, and the only traffic is often a car or two and a cyclist.

The park has a long history of human use. The Timucua people lived here for centuries before the Spanish arrived, and one of their villages, Nocoroco, stood near the river. Later, Europeans established plantations, growing indigo and sugar, and the ruins of old mills and canals still lie in the woods. In the twentieth century, a local artist built a studio here and carved large sculptures that stand near the river, including a figure of a Timucua chief. The landscape is protected now, with trails for walking, a boat ramp and a campground, and canoeing the creeks is a pleasure.

The road through the park is a short, narrow lane, part of the Ormond Scenic Loop, which links the coastal and riverside roads in a ride that feels almost nothing like the rest of the Florida coast. It is shaded and winding by Florida standards, with slow bends, a surface that can be patchy and a canopy that keeps the pavement damp in the morning, so watch for slick patches, sand and fallen branches. t.puschino@54.8,37.6:

t.jerusalem@31.8,35.2:

t.ryazan@54.6,39.7:

At Batambal, as elsewhere, the spheres lie among the low, rounded foundations of the houses and mounds those people built.

Making a perfect ball of stone with no metal tools, and then hauling it across the delta, takes enormous patience, and the finished spheres were evidently important to those who made them. Researchers believe they marked rank and sacred space, not simply decoration, and some seem to have been laid out in relation to each other and the sunrise. The land around is now farmland, but a walk past a sphere in the heat of the day, with the cicadas going, is oddly moving.

The ride in is easy, mostly through the flat farmland south of the mountains, and it is hot. The Pan-American Highway and its side roads pass through fields of palm and rice, with trucks and local buses and the odd cyclist. The Térraba and Sierpe rivers wind through the delta, with mangrove-fringed channels that carry boats towards the Pacific, and the Osa Peninsula lies further south. In the wet season, roads here can flood, and a muddy track can become a puddle on short notice.

Ciudad Cortés has the closest shops, and the larger town of Buenos Aires, about twenty-seven kilometres north, is the safer bet for fuel and a proper meal. Bring water, a hat and a sense of humour about the humidity, and aim to arrive in the morning, when the heat is kind and the light is soft on the stones.

This is the label for the whole collection, and it deserves a longer look: the Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís. UNESCO placed four sites on its World Heritage list in 2014, all within the lower delta of the Térraba river in southern Costa Rica, a few kilometres from Ciudad Cortés. They are the best preserved remains of a culture that thrived here for centuries before European contact, and the reason the word chiefdom appears in the title is that archaeologists see here a society of ranked leaders, craftsmen and farmers, ruled from house-mounds.

The people of the Diquís were skilled potters and goldworkers, and the spheres are their best-known monument. The finest are made of a hard, dark stone, ground and polished until they are almost perfectly round, and they range from fist-sized to well over two metres across. Many were found when the United Fruit Company cleared the land for banana plantations in the 1930s, and some were dragged away and displayed in gardens in San José and around the country, where you can still see them. Their original meaning is lost, but their presence is hard to ignore.

The setting is lowland tropics, wet and flat, ringed by mountains that you can see on a clear morning. The roads are straightforward, the traffic mostly local, and the delta is crossed by wide rivers with muddy brown water that carry the memory of all the rain on the Talamanca range. Heat builds fast after nine, and afternoon downpours are common, so shift your riding to the cool hours and keep your phone dry.

For fuel, rely on Buenos Aires, about thirty kilometres away and the nearest larger town, rather than counting on Ciudad Cortés. Sphere sites can have limited opening hours and entrance fees, and the exact arrangements are best confirmed locally. If you only have time for one site, choose the one with the on-site museum and give the rest a glance from the road, then spend the heat of the day under a tree with a cold drink and a good look at the riverbank.

South of Mitzpe Ramon the Negev stops pretending to be a place of towns and becomes pure geography. This is high desert, around the edge of the great Ramon Crater, a vast erosion valley some forty kilometres long, which geologists call a makhtesh and which exists in only a handful of places in the world. From the lip you look down into a shallow bowl of coloured rock, ochre, black and cream, and the quiet is unusual. The roads are well made and often empty, long grades dropping toward the rift valley of the Arava, and the pace is controlled by the wind, the heat and your fuel. Beirut is a city that has been destroyed and rebuilt many times, and it carries the layers in plain sight. In the modern age, the city was known as the Paris of the Middle East, with cafes, theatres and a cosmopolitan elite, before the civil war of 1975 to 1990 devastated the centre. More recently, a vast explosion at the port in August 2020 killed over two hundred people and damaged much of the city. Recovery is slow, but the city's spirit is strong, and its cooking, from mezze to fresh fish, is justly famous.

Fuel and the supply of electricity have been unreliable in recent years, so check current conditions and fill when you can. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter, snow can close the high passes.
t.gondar@12.6,37.5:
Gondar was Ethiopia's capital for about two hundred years, and it still carries itself like it. Emperor Fasilides founded the city around 1636, and he and his successors built a walled royal compound, the Fasil Ghebbi, filled with stone castles that look as if they belong in medieval Europe, with towers, battlements and arched windows, though the style mixes Ethiopian, Portuguese, Indian and Arab influences. A short distance away lies Fasilides' Bath, a sunken pool inside a walled garden, where each January the Timkat festival sees the water blessed and crowds in white robes jump in. Just outside the centre, the church of Debre Berhan Selassie is covered inside with brilliant seventeenth-century paintings, including a ceiling crowded with winged faces that seem to watch you wherever you stand. It is one of the loveliest church interiors in Africa. The people of the city are mostly Orthodox Christians, and the sound of chanting drifts from the churches at dawn.

The streets are busy with tuk-tuks, minibuses, donkeys and goats, and in the cafés the coffee is served in the traditional ceremony, roasted fresh on a small stove and poured from a clay pot. Start early in the morning, carry plenty of water, and be prepared for sudden rain in the season from June to September. The dry season, from October to March, is the best time to go.
t.chennek@13.3,38.2:
Chennek is a camp on the edge of the world, at around 3,600 metres in the Simien Mountains, where the highland plateau ends in a giant escarpment and drops away for more than a kilometre into the valleys below. The Simien range is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a landscape of towering basalt cliffs, pinnacles and deep gorges that was carved from an enormous volcanic shield, and the views from the rim are among the grandest in Africa. At the south, the highest peak, Ras Dashen, rises over 4,500 metres, one of the highest in the continent.

Gelada baboons, found nowhere else, graze on the grassy slopes in large troops, shuffling along on their bottoms as they pick at the roots and seeds, and the males sport a striking red patch on their chests. The Walia ibex, a rare goat with huge curved horns, lives on the cliffs, and Chennek is one of the best places to see it. Mornings, when the mist lies in the valleys and the sun lights the cliffs, are unforgettable. Come between October and March, when the skies are clear and the rain has gone.
t.naples@26.1,-81.8:
Naples is the end of the Tamiami Trail on the Gulf of Mexico, and after a long ride across the wet flat heart of southern Florida, it can feel almost unreal. The town is a polished, prosperous resort of about twenty-one thousand people with white sand beaches, a long wooden pier, palm-lined avenues, golf courses and some of the most expensive real estate in the state. Retirees, snowbirds and yachts are everywhere, and the air smells of salt and suntan lotion.

It was a monumental piece of engineering for the time, as the road was cut through the Everglades and the Big Cypress swamp, with dredges digging a canal beside it and using the spoil to build the roadbed. It opened in 1928, and the highway transformed southern Florida by connecting the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. The road passes through sawgrass marshes and cypress forest, with canals running alongside, where alligators bask on the banks and herons and egrets stand in the shallows. Thunderstorms burst in the afternoon, and mosquitoes are fierce in the wet season.

The pier has been battered by hurricanes and rebuilt more than once, and in the evenings people gather to watch the sun go down over the gulf. Fresh Gulf seafood is excellent, with stone crab claws in season from October to May, grouper sandwiches and shrimp. Winter, from December to April, is the best time, with mild days, dry weather and clear skies, but it is also the busiest and most crowded.
t.kaluga@54.5,36.3:
Kaluga's most famous resident was a deaf schoolteacher who spent his evenings calculating how a rocket might leave the Earth. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky lived here for decades, teaching mathematics by day and writing on space travel, multi-stage rockets and orbital stations at a time when most people thought the idea absurd. The city is proud of him to a degree that is almost touching: his wooden house is a museum, and the State Museum of the History of Cosmonautics, a large modern building above the Oka, holds rockets, capsules and a remarkable collection of the Soviet space programme's history.

It has around three hundred and forty thousand people, a centre of merchant houses and churches, the long arcaded Gostiny Dvor, and a famous stone bridge across a deep ravine, built in the eighteenth century and still in use as a pedestrian route. Kaluga was also close to a decisive moment in Russian history: in 1480 the armies of Moscow and the Golden Horde faced each other across the Ugra River nearby, and the Tatar withdrawal is traditionally seen as the end of the Mongol yoke.

Riding in, expect city traffic, trolleybuses and some poor surfaces, but also good views of the river as you cross. The real pleasure begins outside: the roads following the Ugra and the Oka run through forest and meadows, with gentle hills, river crossings and long, quiet stretches. Spring brings flooded meadows along the rivers, and early autumn is beautiful, with birch woods turning gold.

The space museum takes a couple of hours if you are interested, and even a short visit is worth it for the sheer strangeness of seeing a Soyuz capsule in a provincial city. The view from the high bank over the Oka at sunset is a good way to end a day, and the city is a sensible base for exploring the Ugra National Park and the land art of Nikola-Lenivets to the west.

The artist Nikolay Polissky started working here with local villagers in the late 1990s, building enormous structures from wood, hay and branches, and the place has since grown into a sprawling park with installations scattered across fields and woods, some playful, some monumental. A summer festival, Archstoyanie, has drawn architects and artists from around the world.

The setting is the Ugra National Park, a protected stretch of river valley with oak and pine woods, flood meadows, sandy beaches and steep banks. The river here is clean and slow, popular for canoeing in summer, and the air smells of hay and pine. In spring the meadows flood and the birds return in huge numbers; in autumn the woods go gold and the mornings are misty. It is a landscape that rewards slowing down.

Getting here is part of the experience. The final approach is on minor roads, sometimes gravel or rough tarmac with potholes, through forest and small villages. Nothing technical, but after rain the dirt sections turn sticky, and on a heavy touring bike some care is needed. Traffic is light except on festival weekends, when the lanes can be crowded with cars and pedestrians. Aim for a weekday in June or September, when the park is quiet and the light is soft.

There is accommodation in and around the park, including some unusual architect-designed cabins, and simple food during the season, but do not count on more. t.ferzikovo@54.5,36.8:
Ferzikovo is a district village of four thousand or so people east of Kaluga, set back from the right bank of the Oka where the river makes its long swing toward Aleksin and Tarusa. Nobody comes here for the village itself, and it would not pretend otherwise: a few streets of wooden and brick houses, an administration building, shops and a church. What makes it a good stopping point is the country around it, which is some of the loveliest along the middle Oka.

The river here runs between high, wooded banks and broad meadows, and the villages along it have that particular central Russian look of grey timber, blue window frames and gardens full of apple trees. This stretch of the Oka attracted painters and writers for a reason. Downstream, between Aleksin and Tarusa, Vasily Polenov built his house and studio on the bank in the late nineteenth century, and the estate, now a museum, is still one of the most beautiful places on the river. Tarusa itself was home to Marina Tsvetaeva in her childhood summers and to Paustovsky later.

There are long views across the valley from the higher ground, especially in the late afternoon when the light comes in low from the west. Traffic is light on weekdays, a little heavier on summer weekends with dacha owners heading out of Kaluga. Watch for loose gravel at junctions and the odd unmarked speed bump through villages.

Practically, Ferzikovo has basic shops and should have fuel on the main road, but for a wider choice of food and services Aleksin, about twenty kilometres away, is the better bet, and Kaluga is around half an hour west. If you are riding on toward Yasnaya Polyana, Tolstoy's estate near Tula, the route continues through farmland and forest. Take a moment on a high point above the Oka before leaving; on a calm summer evening, with the river shining and swallows over the meadows, this is central Russia at its gentlest.
t.apalachicola@29.7,-85.0:

It is level and mostly straight, with long sweeping bends and open views over water. The approach from the east crosses the long bridge over the bay from Eastpoint, and the view of the river mouth and the town's waterfront is lovely. From Eastpoint, a causeway leads out to St. George Island, with wide sandy beaches and a state park.

t.carrabelle@29.9,-84.7:

Camp Gordon Johnston, built here in 1942, prepared tens of thousands of soldiers for beach assaults in Europe and the Pacific, and a small museum in town tells the story with photographs and equipment. Winter is mild, quiet and pleasant, with excellent birdwatching along the shore.
t.ethiopia simien mountains road point 3@1:
Sankaber is where the road stops being a road for most people and becomes a way of seeing the Simien Mountains.

The first thing you notice is the quality of the light, which is thin and clear and makes distances deceptive. The grassland rolls out in wide, pale gold waves, interrupted by clumps of giant lobelia, the tall, spiky plants that grow only on high African mountains, standing like candelabras. In the distance, jagged ridges and flat-topped pinnacles rise out of the haze, and the escarpment falls steeply into valleys so deep that clouds drift beneath your feet. It is a landscape that feels both ancient and slightly unreal.

The people of the area are farmers and herders, and they have lived with the mountains for centuries. Their villages of round huts with thatched roofs sit among terraced fields of barley and wheat, and children and shepherds can appear on the track as you go. Gelada baboons graze on the grass in troops, sometimes close enough to hear them chattering. They are not shy but they are wild, so keep a respectful distance.

It is mostly graded earth and gravel, but ruts, loose stones and washouts are common, especially after rain, and the altitude can sap strength and concentration. A guide or scout is required in the park, and you should check with the park office in Debark about entry rules for motorcycles and conditions before setting out. The dry season, from roughly October to March, is the best time; the wet months can make the track slippery and the views clouded.

There are no towns up here, only small settlements and a few park facilities, so Debark is the supply point. Bring warm clothes, water and a good sense of humour about the weather: it can swing from sun to hail in half an hour.

The cliff edge at Chenek is where the Simien Mountains stop being a landscape and become a drop.

The grassy ledges near the camp are a favourite feeding ground, and large troops move through in the morning and evening, sitting on their haunches and plucking grass blades with fingers that look almost human. Males carry thick manes, and the bare red patch on the chest of both sexes is the reason for the common name 'bleeding-heart baboon'. t.near amman@32.0,35.9:
Amman is the starting point of Jordan's King's Highway, the old road that runs south through the country to the Red Sea, and it is also a city worth a day of its own. It is built on a series of hills, once seven, and the oldest part is the Citadel, which holds the pillars of a Roman temple to Hercules, a Byzantine church and an Umayyad palace, all on the same ridge. The ancient name was Philadelphia, after the Ptolemaic king who rebuilt it, and before that Rabbath Ammon, the capital of the Ammonites. Down in the valley below, a large Roman theatre, carved into the hillside and seating around six thousand people, still stages concerts.

Modern Amman is a young, fast-growing city of over a million people, many of them descended from refugees from Palestine, Iraq and Syria, and it has a lively, welcoming feel. Rainbow Street, with its cafes and old villas, is where people gather in the evening. The downtown souk, near the Roman theatre, is full of spice shops, sweet vendors and coffee sellers, and is the place to try knafeh, a hot cheese pastry soaked in syrup, and hummus with a drizzle of oil, served for breakfast.

Riding in the city is busy but manageable. Drivers are quick and often unpredictable, roundabouts are called circles and numbered, and hills are steep. The roads out are good. The King's Highway heads south through Madaba, famous for its mosaic map of the Holy Land, then down the Wadi Mujib canyon and on to Karak and Petra, with a series of long, winding sections through farmland and desert. It is slower than the fast Desert Highway but far more interesting. In summer the heat is fierce in the south, and in winter rain and even snow can fall on the high ground around Amman.

Fuel and workshops are everywhere, and the city has hotels at every price level. Evenings are cool, even in summer, because of the altitude of about nine hundred metres. Carry water on any journey, and keep your passport and papers accessible for the checkpoints on the main roads. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild days, and the hills around Amman turn green in early spring with a carpet of wildflowers.
t.near petra@30.3,35.4:
Petra is the most famous ruin in Jordan, and it earns the fame. The Nabataeans, an Arab people who grew rich on the incense and spice trade, carved their capital into the rose-coloured sandstone cliffs of a hidden valley more than two thousand years ago. You approach through the Siq, a narrow gorge about a kilometre long, with walls rising on either side until, at the end, the Treasury appears in a slice of light, a monumental facade cut straight out of the rock.

The city declined after the Romans annexed it in the early second century and after earthquakes and shifts in trade routes weakened it. For centuries it was known only to local Bedouin, until the Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812, disguised as a Muslim pilgrim. The poet John William Burgon later called it a rose-red city half as old as time. UNESCO listed the site in 1985, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.

You will probably ride in along the Kings Highway, the old route that runs along the plateau above the Rift Valley from Madaba and Karak in the north to Aqaba in the south. It is one of the great riding roads of the Middle East, with long curves, wide views and fields and villages along the way. Surfaces are generally good on the main route, though goats and slow trucks can appear around any corner, and the weather in winter can be cold with rain and sometimes snow on the high plateau.

The modern town of Wadi Musa lies at the gate of the site and has fuel stations, hotels, cafes and everything a traveller needs. Go into Petra early, because the heat builds fast and the site is huge. The walk to the Monastery is steep, with hundreds of rock-cut steps, but the view at the top is worth it. Take more water than you think you need, and wear shoes you can walk in.
